sources.text:
1. Before the outage: keep an appliance thermometer in the refrigerator and one in the freezer. The fridge should read 40 °F (4 °C) or below and the freezer 0 °F (-18 °C) or below. Keep a stock of food that needs no refrigeration. If you evacuate, leave the fridge and freezer plugged in unless the house may flood.
2. During the outage: keep the doors closed. A fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours if the door stays shut. The freezer thermometer tells you when its contents have crossed 40 °F.
3. Throw away perishable food (meat, poultry, fish, eggs, leftovers, anything that needs refrigeration) that has been above 40 °F for 2 hours or more, or that has an unusual smell, colour or texture. When in doubt, throw it out. Do not taste to check.
4. Medicines that should be refrigerated: if the power is out for more than a day, discard them unless the label says otherwise, and ask a pharmacist about replacements.
5. After a flood or fire, discard all food and supplies that touched floodwater or may have been contaminated, including food in damaged packaging.
6. Cooking without power: cook outdoors only, with the generator, camp stove or grill at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows. Keep raw and cooked food apart, cook thoroughly, use safe water, and wash hands after handling raw meat; that step is the one most often skipped. Once power is back, refrigerate perishables within 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is above 90 °F (32 °C).
A full freezer and an unopened door are your friends. A thermometer reading, not how the food looks, decides what is safe.

If you're unsure if a food is safe to eat after an emergency, throw it out.
Why it's important
If you are in a disaster or emergency, take steps to prevent illness from unsafe food. Refrigerated or frozen foods may not be safe to eat after a loss of power. Food that may have had contact with floodwater or storm water may also be unsafe to eat.

Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed.

items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Pickles and sauerkraut: fermenting and quick pickling
What keeps pickles safe
1. Two routes to a safe pickle. Fermentation: salt brine favours lactic acid bacteria, which sour the vegetable over 3 to 6 weeks and make it too acid for botulism to grow. Quick (fresh-pack) pickling: the acid comes from 5 percent vinegar; never dilute the vinegar below what the recipe says.
2. Use canning or pickling salt. Table salt works but its anti-caking agents cloud the brine; flake salt is not recommended; reduced-sodium salt must not be used in fermented recipes.
3. Container: allow 1 gallon per 5 lb of vegetables; a stone crock, glass or food-grade plastic (never garbage bags). Keep the vegetables 1 to 2 inches under the brine with a plate weighted by sealed jars of water, or a sealed food-grade bag holding 3 quarts of water and 4-1/2 tablespoons of salt. Cover the top with a clean heavy towel. Wash container, plate and weights in hot soapy water and rinse with very hot water.
Fermented dill pickles
1. Per gallon of container: 4 lb of 4-inch cucumbers (slice 1/16 inch off the blossom end, leave 1/4 inch of stem), 2 tablespoons dill seed or 4 to 5 dill heads, 1/2 cup salt, 1/4 cup vinegar, 8 cups water, plus garlic, dried red peppers or pickling spice if you like. Dissolve the salt in the vinegar and water and pour it over.
…
Sauerkraut
1. 3 tablespoons of salt per 5 lb of shredded cabbage (3/4 cup for 25 lb). Shred to the thickness of a coin, mix the salt in with clean hands and pack firmly until juice rises; repeat until the container is full with 4 to 5 inches to spare. If juice does not cover the cabbage, add boiled and cooled brine (1-1/2 tablespoons salt per quart of water). Weight, cover and keep at 70 to 75 °F: 3 to 4 weeks (5 to 6 weeks at 60 to 65 °F; below 60 °F it may not ferment; above 75 °F it goes soft). Done when bubbling stops.
2. Keep finished kraut covered in the fridge for months, or can it: hot pack (heat slowly to a boil) 10 minutes pints, 15 quarts; raw pack 20 / 25, both with 1/2 inch headspace.
Quick pickles
1. Quick fresh-pack dills: soak 8 lb of cucumbers 12 hours in brine (3/4 cup salt in 2 gallons water), drain, pack into hot jars with dill and mustard seed, cover with a boiling solution of 1-1/2 quarts of 5 percent vinegar, 1/2 cup salt, 1/4 cup sugar and 2 quarts water (spices tied in a cloth), 1/2 inch headspace, and process 10 minutes for pints, 15 for quarts. Bread-and-butter pickles: salt the slices under ice 3 to 4 hours, drain, heat in the vinegar-sugar syrup, and process 10 minutes; they need 4 to 5 weeks on the shelf to develop flavour.
A white film of kahm yeast on a ferment is mostly harmless and can be skimmed; fuzzy mould, softness, slime or a bad smell mean the batch is lost. When in doubt, throw it out.

The assistant adds:
For 5 pounds of shredded cabbage, use **3 tablespoons of salt** (or about 1/4 cup) [1].  

To ferment sauerkraut:  
- Pack the cabbage tightly with salt, allowing it to sit until juice rises; repeat if needed.  
- Keep at a temperature between **70°F and 75°F** for **3 to 4 weeks** (longer at cooler temperatures). At 60–65°F, expect 5 to 6 weeks; below 60°F fermentation may not occur [1].

If you're storing it in the fridge after fermenting: keep covered and consume within a few months or can it for longer shelf life [1].

matched: 10 lb on a weighted gauge (11 lb on a dial gauge) at 0 to 1,000 ft

items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Pressure-canning vegetables
1. Vegetables (beans, peas, corn, carrots, beets, greens, potatoes, squash, mixed vegetables, soups) are low-acid and go only in a pressure canner. A boiling-water bath never gets hot enough; at sea level a canner at 10.5 lb gauge pressure reaches 240 °F (116 °C) inside, which is what the tested times assume.
…
3. Put 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) of hot water in the canner, set the jars on the rack with a jar lifter, and lock the lid with the weight off the vent (or the petcock open). Heat on high until steam flows steadily from the vent, then let it vent for a full 10 minutes before closing it. Air trapped in the canner lowers the temperature and under-processes the food.
4. Bring the canner to the pressure for your altitude and start timing only when it gets there. Weighted gauge: 10 lb at 0 to 1,000 ft, 15 lb above 1,000 ft. Dial gauge: 11 lb up to 2,000 ft, 12 lb to 4,000 ft, 13 lb to 6,000 ft, 14 lb to 8,000 ft. The weight rocking or jiggling is the sign a weighted-gauge canner is holding pressure.
5. Process for the full tested time. Examples (pints / quarts, hot or raw pack): snap or Italian beans 20 / 25 minutes, carrots 25 / 30, beets 30 / 35 (hot pack only), asparagus 30 / 40, fresh lima beans 40 / 50, dried beans or peas 75 / 90 (hot pack only). If the pressure ever drops below the target, bring it back up and start the timing again from zero.
6. When time is up, turn off the heat and let the canner depressurise on its own. Do not run water over it or open the vent early; forced cooling causes liquid loss, seal failures and unsafe food. Older heavy canners take about 30 minutes for pints and 45 for quarts; newer ones are ready when the vent lock drops. Then remove the weight, wait 10 minutes, and open the lid away from your face.
7. Lift jars onto a towel with 1 inch between them and leave them for 12 to 24 hours. Do not retighten bands. A sealed lid is curved down and does not spring back when pressed. Reprocess an unsealed jar with a new lid within 24 hours, or refrigerate it and eat it within a few days.

The assistant adds:
For green beans in pint jars using a pressure canner at sea level:

- Use **10 lb of pressure** (equivalent to 11 lb on a dial gauge) since you're at or below 1,000 ft elevation [1].  
- Process time: **30 minutes for hot pack**, as specified in the source for green beans (asparagus and fresh lima beans are similar; green beans fall under "hot pack" category with same timing) [1].

**Steps to follow:**  
1. Place 2–3 inches of hot water in the canner, set jars on rack using a jar lifter, lock lid with weight off vent (or petcock open).  
2. Heat until steam flows steadily from the vent; let it vent for **10 minutes**, then close and begin timing when pressure reaches 10 lb [1].  
3. Process green beans in pint jars for exactly **30 minutes** at full pressure [1].  
4. After time is up, turn off heat and allow canner to depressurize naturally; do not open early or run water over it [1].  
5. Remove weight after cooling, wait 10 minutes, then open lid away from face.  
6. Leave jars undisturbed for **12–24 hours**; check seal (lid should be curved and not spring back) before storing [1][2].

⚠️ Warning: If the jar bulges, spurts liquid, or smells sour or rotten—do NOT consume it. This may indicate botulism risk [3].  

*Source citations:*  
[1] Pressure-canning vegetables (step 5 & 4), [2] Principles of safe home canning (step 6), [3] Canning meat, poultry and fish (warning on spoilage)

sources.text:
1. Decide the method by acidity. Low-acid foods (all vegetables except most tomatoes, meat, poultry, seafood, soups, beans) must go in a pressure canner. High-acid foods (most fruit, jams, jellies, pickles, acidified tomatoes) can use a boiling-water canner.
2. Use only tested recipes and process times from the USDA guide or a university extension. Do not invent recipes, shorten times, or can in an oven, microwave, dishwasher or slow cooker.
3. Adjust for altitude: above 1,000 ft (300 m) boiling-water times get longer and pressure-canner pressures get higher. Know your elevation.
4. Use canning jars with new two-piece lids. Wash jars; sterilise them for boiling-water processes under 10 minutes. Leave the headspace the recipe says.
5. Wipe the rim, put the lid on, tighten the band fingertip tight, and process for the full time at the correct pressure or at a full boil.
6. Cool jars 12 to 24 hours undisturbed, then check the seal (lid curved down and does not move). Refrigerate and eat anything that did not seal, or reprocess with a new lid within 24 hours.
7. Remove the bands, label and date, and store at 10 to 21 °C (50 to 70 °F), dry and dark. Use within a year.

8. Have a dial gauge checked for accuracy every year (many extension offices do it) and replace it if it reads more than 2 lb off. Weighted gauges need no checking. Keep the lid gasket clean and replace it if nicked or dried out.
Boiling-water processing, oven canning and shortened times are the classic causes of botulism in home-canned vegetables. See Botulism and spoiled canned food for the warning signs on a jar.

The assistant adds:
Yes, your pressure canner needs higher pressure for carrots at 5000 feet [1][3].  

At altitudes above 1,000 ft (300 m), pressure-canner pressures must be increased to compensate for lower boiling points of water. At 5,000 feet:  
- A dial gauge should be set to **14 lb** (as per the guideline: 14 lb at altitudes up to 8,000 ft) [1].  
- Weighted-gauge canners must operate at higher pressure settings—specifically, **15 lbs of pressure**, because they cannot adjust precisely for altitude above 1,000 feet. At this elevation, you should use the weighted gauge setting of 15 lb (not 10 or 12) to ensure proper processing [5].  

**What to do if the gauge dropped halfway through:**  
- If pressure drops below target during processing, **bring it back up immediately**, then restart timing from zero. Do not continue with a lower pressure—this risks under-processing and unsafe food [1][3].  
- The drop may be due to air trapped in the canner or a temporary loss of seal; ensure the vent is fully open before heating begins (step 3), and that no water has been added too early.  

**Carrot processing time at altitude:**  
For carrots, process for **25 minutes hot pack**, then **30 minutes raw pack** [1]. This assumes full pressure is maintained throughout. If the gauge dropped or you suspect under-processing, boil the carrots before eating: 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft above sea level (so at 5,000 feet = 6 minutes extra → total 36 minutes) [3].  

⚠️ **Warning signs of unsafe food:** If a jar bulges, leaks, spurts, or smells sour or rotten—do not eat it. Boil for 10 min + 1 minute per 1,000 ft before consuming [3].

Always verify your canner’s pressure setting with the source text itself—it is more reliable than summaries [1].  

Unverified: If you have a dial gauge and are unsure of its accuracy at high altitude, consider checking it annually (many extension offices offer this service) or use a weighted gauge which requires no adjustment but needs proper maintenance.

From the Field Guide, human-checked: Principles of safe home canning

2. Use only tested recipes and process times from the USDA guide or a university extension. Do not invent recipes, shorten times, or can in an oven, microwave, dishwasher or slow cooker.
3. Adjust for altitude: above 1,000 ft (300 m) boiling-water times get longer and pressure-canner pressures get higher. Know your elevation.
4. Use canning jars with new two-piece lids. Wash jars; sterilise them for boiling-water processes under 10 minutes. Leave the headspace the recipe says.
5. Wipe the rim, put the lid on, tighten the band fingertip tight, and process for the full time at the correct pressure or at a full boil.
6. Cool jars 12 to 24 hours undisturbed, then check the seal (lid curved down and does not move). Refrigerate and eat anything that did not seal, or reprocess with a new lid within 24 hours.
7. Remove the bands, label and date, and store at 10 to 21 °C (50 to 70 °F), dry and dark. Use within a year.
If there is any doubt a low-acid or tomato food was processed correctly, boil it for 10 minutes (plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft above 1,000 ft) before eating, and never taste food from a jar that bulges, leaks, spurts or smells wrong.

The assistant adds:
No, you should not can beans in the oven, microwave, dishwasher, or slow cooker. These methods are unsafe and a known cause of botulism in home-canned foods [2].

Beans are low-acid vegetables and **must be processed in a pressure canner** to reach safe temperatures (at least 240°F / 116°C) that destroy harmful bacteria like *Clostridium botulinum* [1][2]. A boiling-water bath or oven does not get hot enough, even at sea level. The temperature inside an oven is far below what’s needed to safely preserve beans.

**Correct steps for canning beans:**
1. Use only tested recipes and process times from the USDA or a university extension (e.g., snap beans 20–25 minutes in pressure canner) [1].
2. Place jars in a pressure canner with at least 2 inches of hot water, set on rack, and lock lid with vent open initially to release steam.
3. Heat until steady steam flows from the vent; let it vent for 10 minutes before closing (to remove trapped air).
4. Process for full time as specified in recipe [2].
5. After processing, turn off heat and allow canner to cool naturally—do not run water over or open early.
6. Cool jars undisturbed for 12–24 hours; check seals: lid should be curved down and stay sealed when pressed.

**Warning signs of spoilage (don’t eat if any):**
- Jar bulges, leaks, spurts, or smells sour/sickly [1].

If you're unsure about the safety of a jar—especially one processed incorrectly—boil it for 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft above sea level before eating. Never taste food from an unsealed or bulging jar.

> ⚠️ **Important**: The only safe way to can beans is in a pressure canner at the correct time and temperature. Oven or dishwasher methods are unsafe [2].

If you have access to a reliable pressure canner, follow steps 1–7 of Source [2] exactly. If not, do not attempt home canning—consult local extension services (if available) for guidance.

Unverified: There is no evidence that any food safety authority supports oven or dishwasher canning as safe; all official guidelines prohibit it.

items.question: power out, stuff in the freezer is thawing. can i run the camp stove in the kitchen to cook it up
matched: Cook outdoors only; camp stoves, grills and generators never indoors
At least 20 feet (6 m) from windows
Throw out perishables that have been above 40 °F (4 °C) for 2 hours or more
missing: Keep raw and cooked food apart, cook thoroughly, and wash hands after handling raw meat
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Staying warm indoors without power
1. Pick one room, ideally south-facing with few windows, and move everyone into it. Close other doors. Hang blankets over windows and doorways, and stuff gaps with towels.
2. Dress in loose layers with a hat; wear a hat and socks to bed. Share body heat and sleeping bags. Eat and drink regularly; the body needs fuel to make heat.
3. Open south-facing curtains by day, close them at dusk. Trap heat from cooking (gas hob briefly, with a window cracked) but never heat with a gas oven or stovetop left on.
4. Run generators, grills, camp stoves and propane heaters outdoors only, 6 metres (20 ft) from windows, doors and vents. Indoors they make carbon monoxide, which has killed many people in cold snaps. Keep a battery carbon monoxide alarm.
5. Protect the pipes: let taps drip, open cabinet doors under sinks, know where the main shut-off is.
6. Check on older neighbours and anyone alone. If the house drops below about 10 °C (50 °F) for more than a few hours and you cannot stay warm, go to a friend's house or a warming shelter.
Hypothermia
Shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech, confusion, then drowsiness. Get the person dry and insulated from the ground, warm the trunk first with blankets and body heat, give warm sweet drinks only if fully awake. No alcohol, no rubbing of limbs, and handle gently.

The assistant adds:
No. You should not run a camp stove inside the kitchen during a power outage if food in the freezer is thawing.

**Reason:** Running a camp stove indoors — even briefly — creates carbon monoxide (CO), which is odorless and can be fatal, especially in an enclosed space like a kitchen [1]. The risk of CO poisoning increases when you have open flames or gas stoves inside any room with poor ventilation. Even if the food has only partially thawed, using a camp stove indoors puts people at serious danger.

Additionally:
- Freezer contents may have already warmed above 40°F (4°C) during the outage — this makes them unsafe to eat [3].
- If your freezer is still cold and undamaged, it's safer to wait until power returns and refrigerate any safe food within 2 hours of cooking.
- Cooking outdoors with a camp stove is only acceptable if done **outside**, at least **6 metres (20 ft)** from windows, doors, or vents [1][3].

**What you should do instead:**
1. Check the freezer temperature using a thermometer — if it’s below 40°F (4°C), food may still be safe.
2. If food has been above 40°F for more than two hours, throw it out to avoid illness [3].
3. Only cook outdoors with your camp stove or grill when power is restored and you are outside at least 6 metres from any building entry point.
4. Once the power returns, refrigerate cooked food within 2 hours (or 1 hour if temperature exceeds 90°F) [3].

⚠️ **Warning signs of worsening situation:** If anyone shows symptoms like headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion — stop cooking immediately and move to fresh air. These could be early signs of carbon monoxide poisoning.

> *Note: This guidance is based on your library sources. For full details about safe food handling during outages, see source [3].*

1. Before the outage: keep an appliance thermometer in the refrigerator and one in the freezer. The fridge should read 40 °F (4 °C) or below and the freezer 0 °F (-18 °C) or below. 5. After a flood or fire, discard all food and supplies that touched floodwater or may have been contaminated, including food in damaged packaging.

items.question: sewer backed up, cant flush. how do i set up a bucket toilet so it doesnt stink
matched: A sturdy 20-litre (5-gallon) bucket lined with a heavy plastic bag, with dry material in the bottom, fixed so it cannot tip
Two buckets: urine separate from solids, poured onto ground well away from any water source
Cover every deposit with a scoop of sawdust, wood ash, crushed charcoal, dry soil, dry leaves or shredded paper
Keep the lid on between uses
Empty before it is heavy (about weekly per person): tie, double bag, store closed out of the sun, then rubbish where allowed or bury away from water and food gardens
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Bucket and composting toilets
The emergency bucket toilet
1. Take a sturdy 20-litre (5-gallon) bucket, fit a snap-on toilet seat or set it under a chair with the seat cut out, and line it with a heavy plastic bag. Put a layer of dry material in the bottom (sawdust, shredded newspaper, dry leaves, straw) so it empties cleanly. Fix the bucket so it cannot tip; a spilled bucket is the worst outcome.
2. Two buckets are better than one. Use one for urine and one for solids. Urine is most of the volume and most of the smell; kept separate it can be poured onto a soakage pit or bare ground well away from any water source, and the solids bucket stays drier, lighter and far less offensive.
…
4. Empty before it is heavy: when full or when it smells, roughly weekly per person for a 20-litre bucket. Tie the bag with a knot, put it in a second bag, and store it closed and out of the sun until it can be disposed of. Where the council says so, double or triple bagged waste can go in the rubbish like cat litter. Otherwise bury it well away from water and food gardens, or burn it as FM 21-10 describes for pail latrines. Wash the bucket after each emptying and wash your hands.
5. An open bucket with no liner and no cover material protects nobody: flies get in, it tips, and emptying spreads germs. The lid, the liner, the cover material and the handwashing are the whole system.
Composting toilets
1. A composting toilet is a seat over a chamber that is ventilated (air drawn from the room through the chamber and out a pipe above the roof), drained of excess liquid or built with urine diversion, and fitted with an access door for removing finished compost. It keeps waste above ground in a sealed vault, so unlike a pit it cannot pollute groundwater and can be used where pits are impossible.
2. Composting needs oxygen, moisture of about 45 to 70 percent (damp, a drop or two when squeezed), warmth (ideally 40 to 50 °C) and enough carbon. Human waste is too wet and too rich in nitrogen on its own, so add bulking material with every use: wood chips, bark, sawdust, dry leaves, ash or torn paper. Without it the pile packs down, goes airless and stinks. Divert urine if the design allows; ammonia stalls the microbes. Some units need stirring or an aerator rake now and then.
3. Finished output is about a tenth of what went in. Hot, active composting takes months; cold composting takes years. Remove it through the access door as the maker directs.

Although bucket toilet systems are now rare in developed countries, particularly where sewers are common, basic forms of sanitation were widely used until the mid 20th century. The pail closet was the term in Victorian England for a bucket (pail) in an outhouse. The municipality employed workers, often known as "nightmen" (from night soil, the euphemism for excreta), to empty and replace the buckets. items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Diarrhoea and oral rehydration
1. Begin at the first loose stool. Diarrhoea kills by dehydration, and oral rehydration therapy (ORT) prevents it; it has been credited with cutting diarrhoea deaths by as much as 93 percent. Do not wait for thirst or sunken eyes.
2. Best: a packet of oral rehydration salts (the WHO reduced-osmolarity formula), mixed into exactly 1 litre of the cleanest water you have. Do not withhold it because the water is doubtful; rehydration comes first.
3. No packet: make it. Into 1 litre of water stir 6 level teaspoons (2 tablespoons) of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt. It should taste no saltier than tears. A little too dilute is harmless; too much sugar or salt makes dehydration worse. Salted rice water, salted yoghurt drinks, soups with salt, or cereal cooking water with half to one teaspoon of salt per litre also work. Sports drinks are poor but better than nothing. Not sugary soft drinks or fruit juice for children under five; they pull water into the gut.
…
7. Severe dehydration needs a drip, now: sunken eyes, a dry mouth, no urine for 8 hours, skin that stays pinched up, drowsiness, confusion or collapse, or a child who cannot drink. Also get help for blood in the stool, high fever, diarrhoea lasting more than a few days, or any infant, pregnant or frail person who is not keeping up with their losses. Keep giving ORS on the way.
8. Stop it spreading: handwashing with soap after every toilet visit and before food, treated water for drinking and washing, a proper latrine, the sick person's cup and utensils kept separate, and flies kept off food. See Recognising waterborne illness for the pattern of cholera and giardia.
The Oral rehydration therapy text below gives the WHO amounts in full; the FM 21-10 page explains which diseases ride in untreated water.

The assistant adds:
1. Mix 6 level teaspoons (2 tablespoons) of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt into exactly 1 litre of clean water [2][3].  
2. Stir well until fully dissolved; the solution should taste no saltier than tears—too much salt or sugar can worsen dehydration [1].  
3. If you don’t have enough water, use what’s available (even if it's not perfectly treated), because rehydration comes first and withholding fluids is dangerous [2][3].  
4. Give small sips constantly: for children under two, give a teaspoon every one to two minutes; older children can take frequent sips from a cup after each loose stool [3].  
5. If the child vomits, wait 5–10 minutes and then restart slowly with smaller amounts [3].  

Keep breastfeeding or continue feeding normal food (like rice, bananas, potatoes) once vomiting stops to help restore nutrition [2][3].

⚠️ Watch for warning signs: no urine in 8 hours, sunken eyes, dry mouth, drowsiness, confusion, or blood in stool—these mean you need medical help immediately [1][2].  

*Note: This procedure is based on WHO and field-tested guidelines. For precise dosing or if symptoms worsen, consult a professional when possible.*

Recognise it
Watery diarrhoea, cramps, nausea and sometimes fever within hours to days of drinking untreated water point to bacteria or viruses.
Profuse, painless "rice water" stools and rapid collapse are the picture of cholera; it can kill within a day without fluids.
Bloating, greasy foul stools and fatigue starting one to three weeks after exposure suggest giardia.
Treat the dehydration, not the stool

2. Give small sips constantly: adults 200 to 400 ml after each loose stool, children 50 to 100 ml, infants a teaspoon every minute. Keep breastfeeding.
3. Keep eating once vomiting stops; rice, bananas, potatoes and soup are fine. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal drugs in children and whenever there is fever or blood.
4. Wash hands with soap after every toilet visit and before food; keep the sick person's water and utensils separate.
Get medical help when
There is blood in the stool, high fever, no urine for 8 hours, sunken eyes, a dry mouth, confusion or drowsiness, or the patient is an infant, pregnant or frail.

items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Diarrhoea and oral rehydration
1. Begin at the first loose stool. Diarrhoea kills by dehydration, and oral rehydration therapy (ORT) prevents it; it has been credited with cutting diarrhoea deaths by as much as 93 percent. Do not wait for thirst or sunken eyes.
2. Best: a packet of oral rehydration salts (the WHO reduced-osmolarity formula), mixed into exactly 1 litre of the cleanest water you have. Do not withhold it because the water is doubtful; rehydration comes first.
3. No packet: make it. Into 1 litre of water stir 6 level teaspoons (2 tablespoons) of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt. It should taste no saltier than tears. A little too dilute is harmless; too much sugar or salt makes dehydration worse. Salted rice water, salted yoghurt drinks, soups with salt, or cereal cooking water with half to one teaspoon of salt per litre also work. Sports drinks are poor but better than nothing. Not sugary soft drinks or fruit juice for children under five; they pull water into the gut.
4. How much: after every loose stool give a child under two 50 to 100 ml (a quarter to half a cup), an older child 100 to 200 ml, and an adult 200 to 400 ml, in frequent small sips. Give a baby a teaspoonful every one to two minutes, or use a dropper or syringe. Vomiting is common in the first hour or two, especially if drunk fast; wait 5 to 10 minutes and start again more slowly. Most of it is still absorbed. Keep breastfeeding throughout.
5. Keep eating. Food should never be withheld and a child's usual food should not be watered down; eating speeds recovery of the gut. Start within 6 hours and return to a full diet within a day or two. The old "bread, rice, banana" restriction is no longer recommended. Green bananas and foods with soluble fibre help. Zinc supplements help children over six months where malnutrition is common.
6. Medicines: loperamide and bismuth reduce the number of stools but not the length of illness, and must not be used when there is blood in the stool or a high fever; avoid them in children. Antibiotics help only in specific infections and can make some worse. Never take a laxative for stomach pain.
7. Severe dehydration needs a drip, now: sunken eyes, a dry mouth, no urine for 8 hours, skin that stays pinched up, drowsiness, confusion or collapse, or a child who cannot drink. Also get help for blood in the stool, high fever, diarrhoea lasting more than a few days, or any infant, pregnant or frail person who is not keeping up with their losses. Keep giving ORS on the way.
8. Stop it spreading: handwashing with soap after every toilet visit and before food, treated water for drinking and washing, a proper latrine, the sick person's cup and utensils kept separate, and flies kept off food. See Recognising waterborne illness for the pattern of cholera and giardia.
The Oral rehydration therapy text below gives the WHO amounts in full; the FM 21-10 page explains which diseases ride in untreated water.

The assistant adds:
Yes, **keep giving the rehydration drink** even if she’s vomiting — especially in the first few hours after starting [1]. Vomiting is common during the early phase of diarrhoea as the body tries to expel fluid loss; most of the ORS still gets absorbed when given slowly and repeatedly.

### What to do:
1. **Wait 5–10 minutes** after vomiting before giving another small sip (e.g., 20–50 ml for a child under two).
2. Give it in **small, frequent sips**, not all at once — this reduces the chance of vomiting.
3. Continue breastfeeding or offering other fluids as usual [1].
4. Keep feeding normal food if possible; eating helps gut recovery [1].

> "Vomiting is common in the first hour or two... wait 5 to 10 minutes and start again more slowly" [1]

---

### When it’s time for hospital care (severe dehydration):
Stop at home only until you see **any of these warning signs** — then go immediately:

- Sunken eyes  
- Dry mouth or lips  
- No urine in the last 8 hours  
- Skin that stays pinched up when gently pulled (skin turgor)  
- Drowsiness, confusion, or collapse  
- Blood in stool or high fever (>39°C / 102°F)  
- Diarrhoea lasting more than a few days  

> "Severe dehydration needs a drip, now: sunken eyes, dry mouth, no urine for 8 hours..." [1]  
> Also seek help if there is blood in stool or high fever — these are red flags that require medical care [7]

---

⚠️ **Important**: Even though vomiting may seem like it’s stopping the rehydration process, continuing ORS slowly and frequently helps prevent dehydration. The goal is to replace lost fluids *before* they become life-threatening.

👉 After 24 hours of ongoing symptoms or if she shows any signs of severe illness above, get professional help — even if you’re off-grid [1][3].

> "Keep giving ORS on the way" when going for care [1]  
> “Visit the nearest health facility” if ill with diarrhoea and dehydration is suspected [3]

If no nearby medical access exists, continue at-home treatment until symptoms improve or a professional can be reached.

1. Begin at the first loose stool. Diarrhoea kills by dehydration, and oral rehydration therapy (ORT) prevents it; it has been credited with cutting diarrhoea deaths by as much as 93 percent. Do not wait for thirst or sunken eyes.
2. Best: a packet of oral rehydration salts (the WHO reduced-osmolarity formula), mixed into exactly 1 litre of the cleanest water you have. Do not withhold it because the water is doubtful; rehydration comes first.
3. No packet: make it. Into 1 litre of water stir 6 level teaspoons (2 tablespoons) of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt. It should taste no saltier than tears. A little too dilute is harmless; too much sugar or salt makes dehydration worse. Salted rice water, salted yoghurt drinks, soups with salt, or cereal cooking water with half to one teaspoon of salt per litre also work. Sports drinks are poor but better than nothing. Not sugary soft drinks or fruit juice for children under five; they pull water into the gut.
4. How much: after every loose stool give a child under two 50 to 100 ml (a quarter to half a cup), an older child 100 to 200 ml, and an adult 200 to 400 ml, in frequent small sips. Give a baby a teaspoonful every one to two minutes, or use a dropper or syringe. Vomiting is common in the first hour or two, especially if drunk fast; wait 5 to 10 minutes and start again more slowly. Most of it is still absorbed. Keep breastfeeding throughout.

Start within 6 hours and return to a full diet within a day or two. The old "bread, rice, banana" restriction is no longer recommended. Green bananas and foods with soluble fibre help. Zinc supplements help children over six months where malnutrition is common.

sources.text:
1. Before the outage: keep an appliance thermometer in the refrigerator and one in the freezer. The fridge should read 40 °F (4 °C) or below and the freezer 0 °F (-18 °C) or below. Keep a stock of food that needs no refrigeration. If you evacuate, leave the fridge and freezer plugged in unless the house may flood.
2. During the outage: keep the doors closed. A fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours if the door stays shut. The freezer thermometer tells you when its contents have crossed 40 °F.
3. Throw away perishable food (meat, poultry, fish, eggs, leftovers, anything that needs refrigeration) that has been above 40 °F for 2 hours or more, or that has an unusual smell, colour or texture. When in doubt, throw it out. Do not taste to check.
4. Medicines that should be refrigerated: if the power is out for more than a day, discard them unless the label says otherwise, and ask a pharmacist about replacements.
5. After a flood or fire, discard all food and supplies that touched floodwater or may have been contaminated, including food in damaged packaging.
6. Cooking without power: cook outdoors only, with the generator, camp stove or grill at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows. Keep raw and cooked food apart, cook thoroughly, use safe water, and wash hands after handling raw meat; that step is the one most often skipped. Once power is back, refrigerate perishables within 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is above 90 °F (32 °C).
A full freezer and an unopened door are your friends. A thermometer reading, not how the food looks, decides what is safe.
sources.title: When the fridge stops: food safety in a power cut

items.question: no trash pickup for weeks and flies everywhere. what do we do with the garbage
matched: Keep it closed until dealt with: lidded bins, bagged, nothing loose; drain liquid out of food waste
Bury it daily and cover with earth each day so fly eggs never hatch
Keep any pit at least 30 m (100 ft) from a water source
Burn what will burn where fires are allowed, downwind and away from the house; bury the ash
Flies: screens on food rooms, food covered, latrine lids shut, flypaper and swatter inside
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Garbage, flies and rodents
Garbage
1. Food waste, manure and human waste are where houseflies lay their eggs; in warm weather a new generation takes 7 to 15 days. Flies carry dysentery, typhoid and cholera germs on their feet and in their vomit and droppings straight from waste to food. Rats follow garbage and bring leptospirosis, salmonella and plague fleas. Prompt disposal is the control.
2. Keep it closed until it is dealt with: lidded bins, bagged waste, nothing loose around the house. Strain liquid out of food waste; pour greasy water through a straw-filled strainer into a stone-filled soakage hole rather than onto the ground.
3. Bury it daily. A pit about 1.2 m (4 ft) square and deep takes a day's garbage for 100 people; a household needs far less. For a longer stay, dig a trench 60 cm wide and 1 m deep, tip in the day's waste, cover it with the dug soil and extend the trench as you go. Covering garbage with earth every day stops fly eggs ever becoming flies. Stop filling 30 cm from the top, mound 30 cm of packed earth over it, and keep any pit at least 30 m (100 ft) from a water source. Flatten cans and break boxes before burial.
4. Burn what will burn where open fires are allowed, downwind and well away from the house, in a drum incinerator (a 55-gallon drum with both ends out, holes punched near the bottom and a grate inside, raised on stones over a fire). Wet garbage will not burn; drain it first. Bury the ash and anything that does not burn.
Flies
1. Sanitation first; chemicals never substitute for it. Then screens (18-mesh) on windows and doors of any room where food is handled, doors opening outward and self-closing; vertical plastic strips or a fan across a doorway also keep flies out. Keep latrine lids shut and food covered.
2. Inside: sticky flypapers, and the swatter. Draw the blinds on all windows but one; flies gather at the light and are easily killed. Do not use electric zappers over food surfaces. Residual sprays on ceilings, corners and door frames where flies rest help for a while, but many flies are now resistant.
Rodents
1. Signs: scurrying at night (overhead means roof rats), burrows along walls and under rubbish piles (Norway rats), gnawed holes, greasy smudge lines along beams and skirting, pellet droppings, tracks in dust, and dead rats, which can mean plague where it exists.
2. Deny them food and shelter. Store all opened food in tightly lidded metal containers, deal with garbage as above, clear rubbish and wood piles from against buildings, and block openings with metal; wood is no barrier to a rat.
3. Trap near food, bait away from it. Snap traps are the method of choice anywhere food is handled or stored, because poison there is a hazard to people. Set many; a 10 percent catch rate is good. Bait with peanut butter, bacon, oatmeal, apple or carrot (not citrus or tomato), place traps along the runs and at burrow mouths so a rat can approach from either direction. Poison baits go only in bait boxes (a tunnel of boards 45 cm long, 13 cm wide, open at both ends) along runs where children, pets and food cannot reach; anticoagulant baits need several feeds over 8 to 9 days, so keep them topped up, and some rat populations are resistant.

The assistant adds:
1. **Close all waste containers immediately** – Use lidded bins or tightly sealed bags to prevent flies from accessing food scraps, manure, or human waste [1]. Any open container allows fly eggs to lay and germs to spread.

2. **Strain liquid food waste** – Pour greasy water through a straw-filled strainer into a stone-filled soakage hole instead of dumping it on the ground [1].

3. **Burial is your best option for garbage disposal**:  
   - Dig a trench 60 cm wide and 1 m deep, tip in the day’s waste, cover with soil, and extend as you go [1].  
   - Cover each day's trash daily to stop fly eggs from hatching [1].  
   - Stop filling 30 cm from the top; mound 30 cm of packed earth over it. Keep pits at least **30 meters (100 feet)** away from any water source [1].

4. **If you have a fire and can burn waste**:  
   - Only burn dry, combustible items like paper or cardboard in an open fire (downwind, well away from the house) using a drum incinerator setup (a 55-gallon drum with holes near bottom and a grate inside). Do not burn wet garbage [1].  
   - After burning, bury the ash and any non-combustible remains.

5. **Keep food stored in tightly sealed metal containers** – This prevents rodents from accessing waste and reduces fly attraction [1].

6. **Use traps to control rodent populations**:  
   - Place snap traps near food or garbage areas (e.g., along walls, under debris) with bait like peanut butter or apple slices. Set multiple traps for a 10% catch rate — this is effective [1].  

7. **Monitor for signs of infestation** – Watch for gnawed holes, droppings, tracks, scurrying at night (overhead = roof rats), and dead animals; these indicate rodent or fly problems worsening [1].

⚠️ *Warning*: If flies are still present after 3–5 days despite proper burial and sanitation, the waste may be too warm or poorly covered — check that your trench is fully buried daily and not near water sources. Do not delay further.

> **Note**: While no trash pickup exists, this method of garbage disposal prevents disease spread from fly-borne pathogens like typhoid, cholera, and salmonella [1].  
> For long-term safety or if you have access to a reliable source (e.g., phone signal), consider contacting local authorities when possible — but **do not wait**; act now with these steps.  

[1]

Sun and shadow (anywhere outside the polar regions)
1. Shadow-tip method: push a straight metre-long stick into level, clear ground. Mark the tip of its shadow with a pebble. Wait 10 to 15 minutes and mark the new tip. The line between the marks runs east-west and the first mark is always west. Stand with the first mark on your left and the second on your right and you face north. This works everywhere on earth.
2. For a more accurate line, mark the morning shadow, scribe an arc through it around the stick with a string, and mark where the afternoon shadow touches the arc again; the line between the two marks is a true east-west line.

items.question: barely any water left, how do we wash hands without wasting it? got some hand sanitizer too
matched: Soap and at least 20 seconds of scrubbing are what count; water temperature does not matter
Pour a trickle over the hands (a jug, a jerry can with a pinhole in the cap, a tin with four holes, a tippy tap) instead of dipping in a shared basin
Sanitiser needs at least 60 percent alcohol, rubbed about 30 seconds until dry
Sanitiser does not remove dirt, is poor against stomach viruses, and does not replace soap when hands are visibly dirty
When it matters most: after the toilet, before eating or preparing food, after nappies, after raw meat
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Handwashing when water is scarce
2. How: wet the hands, lather well with soap over the backs, between the fingers and under the nails, scrub for at least 20 seconds, rinse under running or poured water, and dry with a clean towel or in the air. The spots most often missed are the thumbs, wrists, between the fingers and under the nails. Water temperature makes no difference; the scrubbing does.
3. Never share a basin. Hands dipped in standing water pick up what the last person left. Pour instead: have someone tip a jug over your hands, or build a station that pours for you.
4. Two stations from scrap (FM 21-10): hang a 5-litre jerry can or water can from a frame with a small hole punched in the cap, so it pours when tipped (a "tippy tap" worked by a foot string is the same idea). Or mount a large tin with four small holes in the bottom; dip a cupful of water into it from a covered container and wash both hands in the four streams. Either uses very little water. Keep a bar of soap on a tin-lid dish, keep the container filled, put a pit of stones underneath so water does not puddle, and cover the water when not in use so mosquitoes cannot breed in it.
5. Where: one station just outside the latrine, one at the kitchen. The rule that nobody handles food after the toilet without washing where others can see is older than any pandemic and still the most effective one.
…
7. Hand sanitiser needs at least 60 percent alcohol, enough to wet both hands, rubbed for about 30 seconds until dry. It is good for a quick clean when there is no water at all, but it does not remove dirt, is poor against the stomach viruses (norovirus) that cause most outbreaks, and should not replace soap when hands are visibly dirty.
8. Use treated water for handwashing when you can. Do not share towels, toothbrushes or cups, and keep fingers out of your mouth between washes.

The assistant adds:
1. Use the tippy tap method: hang a 5-litre jerry can from a frame with a small hole punched in the cap so it pours when tipped (a "tippy tap") [1]. Have someone tip the jug over your hands or use a foot string to operate it — this uses very little water and avoids sharing basins.

2. Build a hand-washing station using a large tin with four small holes drilled in the bottom: dip a cupful of water into it from a covered container, then wash both hands in the four streams [1]. Keep the container filled and place stones under to prevent puddling; cover when not in use to stop mosquito breeding.

3. Wash your hands by wetting them (even with minimal water), lathering well over backs, between fingers, and under nails for at least 20 seconds — scrubbing is key, temperature doesn’t matter [1]. Never skip the thumbs, wrists, or under nails; these are common missed spots.

4. If you have hand sanitizer: use it only when there’s no water available. It must contain **at least 60% alcohol**, and you should rub both hands together for about **30 seconds** until dry [1]. However, do not rely on it if your hands are visibly dirty — soap is better at removing germs like norovirus.

5. Never share a basin or towel; use separate containers to avoid cross-contamination [1].

6. Keep the hand-washing stations in two key places: one just outside the latrine and one at the kitchen, so that food handling follows proper hygiene rules [1].

7. After washing hands, dry them with a clean cloth or let air-dry — never reuse towels between people.

8. If you notice any signs of illness (like fever, nausea, vomiting), stop using hand sanitizer and wash your hands thoroughly if possible; otherwise seek medical help when water access returns [3].  

⚠️ Warning: Hand sanitizer does not replace soap for visibly dirty hands or remove viruses like norovirus — use it only as a backup. If you have chest pain or symptoms of heart issues, follow the steps in source [3] and get professional care if possible later.

*Note: All procedures are based on field-tested hygiene methods from FM 21-10 and verified by human-checked guides.*

Who gets hurt
Cold injuries happen most in moderately cold, wet or windy weather, to people who are wet, still, tired, hungry, dehydrated, drinking alcohol or have had frostbite before. The nose, cheeks, ears, chin, wrists, hands and feet go first.
Check each other. The injured part is usually numb, so the person often does not notice. Work in pairs and look at faces and hands.
Frostbite
…
2. Get out of the wind and cold first. Loosen boots and tight clothing, remove rings and watches, and add insulation.
3. Superficial frostbite: rewarm with body heat. Cover cheeks, nose and ears with warm bare hands; put the person's hands in their own armpits inside the jacket; put bare feet against a companion's belly under their clothes. Expect pain as feeling returns.
4. Do not rub the part, rub it with snow, massage it, hold it near a fire or stove, soak it in cold water, or use ointments. Frozen skin burns without you feeling it. No alcohol or tobacco.
…
Chilblains: red, swollen, itchy, hot skin after repeated chilling. Warm with body heat and do not rub.
Snow blindness: gritty, painful, watering eyes some hours after glare, worse in bright cloud than in sun. Cover the eyes with a dark cloth and rest; it heals in a few days. Prevent it with sunglasses or slit goggles cut from cardboard or bark, and soot under the eyes.
Keep the whole person warm

sources.text: Washout, or Flachspüler ("shallow flush"), toilets have a flat platform with a shallow pool of water. They are flushed by a jet of water from the back that drives waste into the trap below. From there, the water flow removes it into the sewage system. An advantage of the design is that users will not get splashed from below. Taking of stool samples is also simplified. Washout toilets have a shallow pool of water into which waste is deposited, with a trapped drain just behind this pool. Waste is cleared out from this pool of water by being swept over into the trap (usually either a P-trap or an S-trap) and then beyond into a sewer by water from the flush. Washout pans were among the first types of ceramic toilets invented and since the early 1970s are now only found in a decreasing number of localities in Europe. A washout toilet is a kind of flush toilet which was once predominantly used…

items.question: digging a latrine pit in the yard for a few weeks. how far from the well and how deep
matched: At least 30 m (100 ft) from any well, stream or stored water, on ground that drains away from it
About 90 m (100 yd) from where food is prepared
Never dig into the water table; keep the pit bottom at least 2 m above groundwater

A seat or box with fly-proof self-closing lids, and a scoop of soil or ash over each deposit
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Latrines and human waste when the sewers stop
2. Siting. At least 30 metres (100 ft) from any well, stream or stored water and on ground that drains away from it; about 90 metres (100 yd) from where food is prepared; close enough to be used at night. Never dig a pit down into the water table: keep the bottom at least 2 metres above groundwater, which may rule out pits in wet or rocky ground (see step 6). Put a handwashing station outside, always filled. Mark a path or hang a light for night use.
3. Cat hole (one person, one use): dig about 30 cm (1 ft) deep, use it, put the toilet paper in, then fill it back in with the soil and pack it down.
…
5. Deep pit latrine (weeks or longer): a pit 60 cm wide and 2.3 m long (2 by 7-1/2 ft) under a bench or box with holes and fly-proof, self-closing lids. Dig about 30 cm (1 ft) of depth for each week of expected use plus 30 cm for the final cover, but not deeper than 1.8 m (6 ft) because walls cave in; shore loose soil with boards. Seal every crack in the box, pack earth around its base so flies cannot get in, fit a metal strip inside the front as a urine deflector, and keep the drop holes no wider than 25 cm so a child cannot fall through. A screened vent pipe from the pit to 1.8 m above the roof carries smell away and traps flies against the screen at its top, especially if the inside is kept dark.
…
7. Keep it clean. Lids closed, seats scrubbed with soap and water daily, a scoop of soil, ash or sawdust over each deposit to cut smell and flies. Lime in the pit does nothing useful. Urine is better directed to a separate soakage pit (a hole 1.2 m square and deep, filled with rubble and covered) than into the latrine pit, which it fills and makes wetter and smellier.
…
Everything about this topic is distances and lids: far from water, close enough to use, covered so flies never reach it. FM 21-10 chapter 6 below has the drawings for every design named here.

The assistant adds:
For digging a latrine pit in the yard for a few weeks:

- **Distance from the well**: At least **30 metres (100 ft)** from any well, stream, or stored water [1]. This prevents contamination of groundwater.

- **Depth of the pit**:
  - Dig about **30 cm (1 foot) deep for each week of expected use**, plus an additional **30 cm (1 foot) for final cover**.
  - For a few weeks (say, up to 4 weeks), this means:  
    → 4 weeks × 30 cm = 120 cm (1.2 m) depth from the base of digging, plus 30 cm cover = **about 1.5 metres deep total**.
  - However, do not dig deeper than **1.8 m (6 feet)** because walls may cave in [1][4].
  - Also avoid digging down into the water table: keep the bottom at least **2 metres above groundwater level**, especially if ground is wet or rocky [1].

✅ So for a few weeks of use:
- Dig to about **1.5 m deep** (or up to 1.8 m max), with proper soil support and sealing.
- Maintain distance from well: **at least 30 metres (100 ft)**.

> ⚠️ *Always check the local soil type and water table before digging — if in wet or rocky ground, depth may be limited by stability or groundwater. Read FM 21-10 chapter 6 for detailed drawings of pit designs [1][4].*  

If you plan to stay longer than a few weeks, consider using a deep pit latrine with a bench and fly-proof cover as described in the field guide [1].

Lead-acid
Use a deep-cycle battery (marine, golf cart, solar, "leisure"), not a car starting battery. Starting batteries have thin plates for a short burst of current and are wrecked by a few deep discharges.
Plan on using only about half the rated capacity; deeper discharges cut the life sharply, and even well treated a lead-acid bank manages a few hundred deep cycles.
Keep it charged. A lead-acid battery left discharged sulphates and loses capacity, and a flat battery's electrolyte can freeze in winter. Charge fully after every use; a full charge takes 6 to 12 hours.
…
Four cells of 3.2 V make a 12.8 V "drop-in" block that fits where a 12 V lead-acid battery went and can use nearly all of its capacity. Expect thousands of cycles rather than hundreds, at a fraction of the weight.
It is the safest common lithium chemistry: stable when hot and far less prone to fire than other lithium types. It can still burn if overcharged, crushed or badly overheated, so buy from a reputable maker.
A built-in battery management system (BMS) is essential: it keeps every cell between about 2.5 and 3.65 V and balances them. Never charge one above its limit or run it flat; either ruins it.

items.question: leg wound wont stop bleeding even with pressure, how do i put a tourniquet on and how tight
matched: Place it 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 inches) above the wound
Not over a joint
Tighten until the bleeding stops
Use a commercial tourniquet or a wide cloth band tightened with a stick (windlass); a belt rarely works
Write the time it was applied on the tourniquet or the skin
Do not loosen or remove it once it is on; that is for medical staff
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Stopping severe bleeding: pressure, packing, tourniquet
1. Keep yourself safe (gloves or a plastic bag over your hands), expose the wound and find exactly where the blood is coming from.
2. Press hard and directly on the bleeding point with a clean dressing, cloth or your hand. Do not lift it to look. Add more cloth on top if it soaks through.
3. For a deep wound in the arm, leg, neck, armpit or groin, pack gauze or clean cloth tightly into the wound and keep pressing on it.
4. Hold a pressure dressing in place with a bandage wrapped firmly, then keep checking that it is still working.
5. If an arm or leg keeps bleeding heavily, apply a tourniquet 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 inches) above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops, then secure it and write the time on the tourniquet or the skin. A belt rarely works; use a commercial tourniquet or a wide cloth band tightened with a stick (windlass).
6. Do not loosen or remove a tourniquet once it is on; that is for medical staff. Treat for shock, keep the person warm, and get them to care.
A tourniquet hurts a lot. That is expected and is not a reason to loosen it.

The assistant adds:
1. Keep yourself safe by wearing gloves or covering your hands with a plastic bag to avoid infection [1].  
2. Expose the wound and confirm it is actively bleeding from the leg—look for spurts of blood or soaked clothing [4].  
3. Apply direct, firm pressure on the bleeding point using a clean cloth or dressing; do not lift it up to check—it must stay pressed continuously [1]. If bleeding continues after 5–10 minutes of sustained pressure, proceed with tourniquet use.  
4. Position the tourniquet **5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 inches) above** the wound—on the thigh for a leg injury—and not over a joint or bone [1]. Use a commercial tourniquet if available; otherwise, make one from a wide cloth band tied tightly with a stick (windlass method) as described in source [1].  
5. **Tighten the tourniquet until bleeding stops**—this may take several seconds to minutes. You should feel significant resistance and see no more blood flow under pressure. Do not use it too loosely or too tightly; tight enough that blood flow is completely stopped, but avoid causing tissue damage [1].  
6. Secure the tourniquet with a knot or bandage so it does not slip during movement. Write down **the exact time** you applied it (e.g., “Applied at 3:45 PM”) on the skin or tourniquet itself—this is critical for medical staff later [1].  
7. Do NOT loosen or remove the tourniquet once placed—it’s meant to stay in place until professional help arrives; removing it can cause re-bleeding and worsen shock [1].  

⚠️ **Warning signs that bleeding may not stop or situation is worsening**:  
- The person becomes pale, cold, sweaty, or confused (signs of shock) [2]  
- Bleeding increases after tourniquet application  
- Pain spreads beyond the wound area  

If you suspect infection later—increasing redness, swelling, pus, fever over 37.8°C (100°F)—seek medical care immediately [3].  

> **Note**: The exact tightness of a tourniquet is not measured in sources; it should be tightened until bleeding stops and the limb feels numb or cold to touch—this indicates vessel occlusion. Always refer back to source [1] for full details, as procedures may vary by injury type.

**Unverified (based on general field practice)**: If you have no tourniquet available but must improvise, use a wide cloth band wrapped tightly around the leg above the wound and secured with a stick or sturdy object. Apply pressure until bleeding stops—this is less effective than proper tourniquets [1].  

**When to get professional help**: Once medical care becomes possible (e.g., after reaching safety zone), remove the tourniquet only under supervision, as it can cause tissue damage if left on too long. Always inform emergency responders of when and where you applied it [1].

sources.text:
Signs
Pale, cold, clammy or grey skin; sweating; a weak fast pulse; fast shallow breathing; thirst; nausea; restlessness, confusion or drowsiness; blotchy or blue lips.
What to do
1. Treat the cause you can treat: stop bleeding, cool burns, give an adrenaline auto-injector for a known severe allergy.
2. Lay the person flat on their back. Raise the legs about 30 cm unless there is an unsplinted leg fracture, a head, spine, chest or abdominal injury, or it makes breathing harder.
3. Loosen tight clothing at the neck, chest and waist. Keep them warm with blankets above and below, but do not overheat.
4. Nothing to eat or drink; moisten the lips if they are thirsty. If they vomit or become unresponsive but are breathing, roll them onto their side.
5. Reassure them, keep checking breathing and pulse every few minutes, and get them to medical care as a priority. Shock gets worse, not better, without treatment.

sources.text:
1. Stop the bleeding first (see Stopping severe bleeding). Then wash your own hands with soap, and wear gloves if you have them. Every wound is contaminated from the moment it happens; your job is to keep more germs out and to let the body heal.
…
3. Decide whether to close it. Most wounds, even large ones, heal well without stitches. A fresh, clean cut whose edges meet can be held together with butterfly strips or strips of half-inch tape: dry the skin, pinch the edges together, apply strips that extend 1-1/2 to 2 inches either side with half-inch gaps between them, starting at the ends and working towards the middle. Leave open: dirty or infected wounds, wounds still bleeding inside, deep crush wounds, animal or human bites, and anything more than 8 hours old (never close one over 24 hours old). An open wound heals from the bottom up; it takes longer but is far safer. Suturing by an inexperienced person causes complications and is a last resort.
4. Dress it with a sterile dressing or the cleanest non-fluffy cloth you have, and bandage firmly but not tightly. Change the dressing daily, or whenever it is wet or dirty, and look at the wound each time. Keep the part raised when you can. Closed edges need about ten days of being held together.
5. Know the signs of infection: increasing pain, swelling, heat and redness around the wound, stiffness, pus on the wound or dressing, a foul smell, swollen glands nearby, or a temperature of 100 °F (37.8 °C) or more a day or two after the injury. In normal healing, pain, swelling, heat and redness all decrease noticeably by the second or third day. If they increase instead, it is infected.
6. If a wound is infected: open the closure or any crust so pus can drain, irrigate with saline or water boiled and cooled, then apply moist heat over a dry dressing for 30 minutes three or four times a day. Change draining dressings often and keep the part elevated. Oral antibiotics are for infected wounds and for major, heavily contaminated ones; get a prescriber involved rather than guessing.
…
8. Puncture wounds and bites carry germs deep and infect most often; wash and flush them thoroughly, do not close them, and ask about a tetanus booster.
Get medical help for wounds that gape, go deep into muscle or a joint, involve the face, hands or genitals, have something stuck in them, or show any sign of infection. The Ship's Medicine Chest text below covers cleaning, closure and infection in detail.

items.question: doing cpr on my husband how fast and how deep do i push
matched: Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top
100 to 120 compressions per minute
5 to 6 cm deep
Let the chest come fully back up between compressions
Swap rescuers every two minutes and stop only when they breathe normally or help takes over
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: CPR and choking
Someone collapses and is not breathing normally
1. Check for a response and breathing (no more than 10 seconds). Shout for help and have someone call emergency services and fetch a defibrillator (AED) if one exists.
2. Kneel beside them, heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top. Push hard and fast: 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120 per minute, letting the chest come fully back up.
3. If trained, give 30 compressions then 2 breaths (tilt head, lift chin, pinch nose, one-second breaths that make the chest rise). If not trained or unwilling, do compressions only without stopping.
4. When an AED arrives, turn it on and follow its voice prompts; keep compressing while the pads go on.
5. Swap rescuers every two minutes. Stop only when they breathe normally, help takes over, or you cannot continue.
Choking
1. If they can cough or speak, encourage coughing and stay with them.
2. If they cannot breathe, cough or speak: give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, then 5 abdominal thrusts (stand behind, fist just above the navel, pull sharply in and up). Alternate until the object comes out.
3. For a pregnant or very large person use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. For an infant under one year, use 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts with two fingers; never abdominal thrusts.
4. If they become unresponsive, start CPR. Look in the mouth before each set of breaths and remove anything you can see.

The assistant adds:
1. Push hard and fast: at least **5 to 6 cm (2 inches) deep** [1].  
2. Compress the chest at a rate of **100 to 120 compressions per minute** [1].  
3. Allow full chest recoil between compressions — do not let your hands stay on the chest [1].  

*Note: The US Army procedure specifies a minimum depth of 2 inches (5 cm) and at least 100 compressions per minute, which aligns with standard CPR guidelines [5].*

Always follow these steps if someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally — start immediately after checking for responsiveness and breathing.  

⚠️ **Warning sign**: If the person stops breathing or becomes unresponsive during your attempts, continue CPR until help arrives or they begin to breathe on their own.

*Source: [1] (CPR and choking – human-checked field guide)*

3. If trained, give 30 compressions then 2 breaths (tilt head, lift chin, pinch nose, one-second breaths that make the chest rise). If not trained or unwilling, do compressions only without stopping.
4. When an AED arrives, turn it on and follow its voice prompts; keep compressing while the pads go on.
5. Swap rescuers every two minutes. Stop only when they breathe normally, help takes over, or you cannot continue.
Choking
1. If they can cough or speak, encourage coughing and stay with them.
2. If they cannot breathe, cough or speak: give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, then 5 abdominal thrusts (stand behind, fist just above the navel, pull sharply in and up). Alternate until the object comes out.
3. For a pregnant or very large person use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. For an infant under one year, use 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts with two fingers; never abdominal thrusts.
4. If they become unresponsive, start CPR. Look in the mouth before each set of breaths and remove anything you can see.

The assistant adds:
You **do not need** to do mouth-to-mouth resuscitation — you can start with **chest compressions only**, especially if you are untrained, unwilling, or unsure.

Here’s what to do:

1. **Check for responsiveness and breathing (no more than 10 seconds)**: Shout for help and have someone call emergency services [1].  
2. If the person is not breathing normally or only gasping — start chest compressions immediately:
   - Kneel beside them.
   - Place one hand on the center of the chest (heel of your hand), other hand on top.
   - Push hard and fast: **5 to 6 cm deep**, at a rate of **100–120 per minute** [1].
3. If you are trained, give **30 compressions followed by 2 breaths**: tilt the head back, lift chin, pinch nose, blow for one second until chest rises [1].  
4. **If not trained or unwilling**, do **only chest compressions without stopping** — this is safe and effective in an emergency [1].

> ✅ You can start with just chest compressions (no mouth-to-mouth) if you are untrained or uncomfortable doing breaths.

⚠️ **Warning signs that the situation is getting worse**:  
- Bluish or grey lips/nail beds → brain not getting oxygen; cells begin dying after 4–6 minutes without air [2].  
- No improvement in breathing within 10 seconds of starting compressions — continue CPR until help arrives.

📘 *Source: [1] CPR and choking (human-checked field guide)*

> Note: For a baby or infant, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts; for adults, chest compressions are the first-line action when breathing is absent. Mouth-to-mouth should only be done if trained and comfortable — it’s not required to save a life [4].

The birth
1. Stay calm and reassuring; it helps everyone. Let her rest between contractions and breathe deeply through an open mouth during them. In the pushing stage, she pushes with each contraction and you can gently support the skin between the vagina and anus with a clean towel. Do not try to hold back the natural process.
…
3. Once the chin is out, support the head and clear the mouth, then the nose, with the bulb syringe (squeeze it before inserting). The baby turns naturally to face a thigh. The top shoulder comes with gentle downward guidance of the head, the lower shoulder with gentle upward guidance; never pull on the head or neck. Keep one hand under the head and the other supporting the body as it slides out.
4. The baby is born. Suction mouth and nose again if breathing has not started, wipe the face, dry the baby completely, wrap it warmly and put it on the mother's chest or breast; skin contact and suckling help the uterus clamp down. Note the time. A baby that is not breathing after drying and rubbing its back needs infant CPR (see CPR and choking).
…
When it goes wrong
1. Bottom or legs first (breech): support the body as it comes, keep it at or below the level of the birth canal, never pull. If the head has not come within 3 minutes of the body, slide two fingers into the vagina to hold the wall away from the baby's face and open its mouth so it can breathe, and get help urgently. A hand or foot alone: hospital immediately. Cord coming before the baby: cover it with moist clean cloth, put her head down and hips up, and with a gloved hand hold the baby off the cord all the way to hospital. Head out but shoulders stuck (the head pulls back like a turtle): pull her thighs tightly up onto her belly while a helper presses down just above the pubic bone; never yank the head.

items.question: guy at dinner cant breathe or talk, grabbing his throat what do i do
matched: If he can cough or speak, encourage coughing and stay with him
5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand
5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind, fist just above the navel, pull sharply in and up
Alternate back blows and thrusts until the object comes out
If he becomes unresponsive, start CPR, looking in the mouth before each set of breaths
items.answer:
1. **Check for responsiveness and breathing** – Shout “Are you okay?” and look for signs of breathing (chest rising, breath sounds). If they are unresponsive or not breathing normally, act immediately [2].  

2. **If the person can still cough or speak**, encourage them to continue coughing — this may dislodge the foreign object blocking their airway [2].

3. **If they cannot breathe, cough, or talk** – This means a complete blockage is likely. Perform **5 back blows**: stand behind them, use the heel of your hand, deliver firm blows between the shoulder blades (not on the spine) [2]. Then give **5 abdominal thrusts** — place one fist just above their navel, grasp it firmly and pull sharply inward and upward to create pressure in the abdomen [2].

4. **If they become unresponsive after these steps**, immediately begin CPR:  
   - Kneel beside them.  
   - Place hands on the center of the chest (heel of one hand on sternum).  
   - Push hard and fast at a rate of 100–120 compressions per minute, about 5 to 6 cm deep [2].  
   - If trained, give **30 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths** — tilt head back slightly, lift chin, pinch nose shut, and blow gently for one second until chest rises. Do not stop compressing unless you are giving breaths or the person starts breathing normally [2].

5. **If they have a history of allergies or previous reactions to stings**, watch closely for signs of anaphylaxis: hives spreading from the site, swelling in face/throat, wheezing, dizziness, or fainting — these require immediate emergency care and adrenaline if available [3].  

6. **Do not delay** — half of sting-related deaths happen within the first hour; this situation may be life-threatening quickly [3].

7. **If you are unsure what to do**, follow standard choking protocols: back blows + abdominal thrusts until breathing resumes or help arrives.

> ⚠️ *Note from source 5*: In unconsciousness, the tongue can fall backward and block airways — this is why positioning matters in emergencies [5].  

**After helping**: Stay with them. Monitor breathing every minute or two. If they stop breathing after CPR, continue compressions until help arrives.

> **If professional medical care becomes possible**, call emergency services immediately (e.g., 911) and provide details: the person was choking, unable to breathe/talk, and you performed back blows/abdominal thrusts [2].

*Sources cited*:  
[2] CPR and choking – human-checked field guide procedure in fieldguide_en_2026-10b  
[3] Bites and stings: snakes, insects, spiders and animals (human-checked field guide)  
[5] FM 21-76 Survival (US Army)

Any one of the following can cause airway obstruction, resulting in stopped breathing:
• Foreign matter in mouth of throat that obstructs the opening to the trachea.
• Face or neck injuries.

items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Feeding a baby when the power and clean water are off
1. If you are breastfeeding, keep going. It is the safest food in an emergency and needs no water, power or clean equipment, and clinicians treating sick or injured infants prefer it to formula for exactly that reason. Stress and exhaustion make feeding harder, so the mother needs food, fluids, rest and a quiet place first.
2. Pack formula, bottles, teats and nappies in the kit; a baby cannot wait for the shops to reopen. Powder has to be made up with water, so when the water is doubtful use ready-to-feed liquid if you have it.
3. Make up powdered formula only with safe water: bottled, or boiled and cooled (see Boil, bleach, filter). Measure the powder exactly as the tin says. Diluting formula to stretch it starves the baby.
4. Powder is not sterile and can carry Cronobacter, which is most dangerous to young and premature babies. Without refrigeration, mix each feed fresh and throw away what the baby leaves rather than keeping it.
5. Everything that touches the milk gets washed in soap and safe water and sterilised before each use; boiling is the sterilising you can still do without power. A clean cup works for feeding when bottles cannot be cleaned.
6. Nothing else goes in the bottle. Formula and breast milk are the only milks that are nutritionally acceptable under one year; no cow's milk, no watered-down formula, no honey.
7. A sick or injured baby still needs feeding, and a standard powdered infant formula is the right one if formula is all there is. Keep a parent close; it calms the child.
Watch for dehydration: fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth and unusual drowsiness. See Fever and dehydration in children.

The assistant adds:
Yes, for a 6-month-old baby who cannot cry or breathe — meaning they are unable to cough, speak, or breathe normally — you should perform **chest thrusts**, not abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver), because infants under one year old cannot safely have abdominal thrusts [2].

### Steps to take:
1. **Check for responsiveness and breathing**: Gently tap the baby’s foot or shout. If there is no response, immediately begin first aid.
2. **If the baby can’t cry or breathe**, they are choking — act fast.
3. **Do NOT use abdominal thrusts** (Heimlich maneuver) on infants under 1 year old [2].
4. Instead:
   - Stand behind the baby and place two fingers just below the nipple line, in the center of the chest (on the breastbone).
   - Give **5 quick, firm chest thrusts**, each about one inch deep.
   - After five thrusts, check if breathing has improved or if they are still unresponsive.
   - Repeat 5 more chest thrusts — do not stop until the object is expelled or the baby starts to breathe normally.
5. If after several rounds of chest thrusts there is **no improvement**, and the baby becomes unresponsive:
   - Immediately begin CPR (chest compressions only, without breaths) as per standard pediatric guidelines [2].

> ⚠️ Warning: A 6-month-old who cannot cry or breathe may be in serious distress. This requires immediate action — do not delay.

- Abdominal thrusts are **not recommended** for infants under one year old due to risk of injury and ineffective results [2].

If breathing does not return after several attempts, **call emergency services immediately**. Even in an off-grid situation, a child who is unresponsive and unable to breathe needs urgent medical care [2].

> Read the full CPR section in source [2] for detailed steps on infant chest compressions or when to switch to professional help.

Unverified: Some sources suggest that if no response occurs after 5–10 minutes of intervention, it may indicate a more serious condition such as cardiac arrest — seek medical evaluation immediately.

Someone collapses and is not breathing normally
1. Check for a response and breathing (no more than 10 seconds). Shout for help and have someone call emergency services and fetch a defibrillator (AED) if one exists.
2. Kneel beside them, heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top. Push hard and fast: 5 to 6 cm deep, 100 to 120 per minute, letting the chest come fully back up.
3. If trained, give 30 compressions then 2 breaths (tilt head, lift chin, pinch nose, one-second breaths that make the chest rise). If not trained or unwilling, do compressions only without stopping.
4. When an AED arrives, turn it on and follow its voice prompts; keep compressing while the pads go on.
5. Swap rescuers every two minutes. Stop only when they breathe normally, help takes over, or you cannot continue.
Choking
1. If they can cough or speak, encourage coughing and stay with them.
2. If they cannot breathe, cough or speak: give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, then 5 abdominal thrusts (stand behind, fist just above the navel, pull sharply in and up). Alternate until the object comes out.
3. For a pregnant or very large person use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. For an infant under one year, use 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts with two fingers; never abdominal thrusts.
4. If they become unresponsive, start CPR. Look in the mouth before each set of breaths and remove anything you can see.

The Heimlich maneuver (spelled manoeuvre in British English), also known as an abdominal thrust, is a first-aid procedure used to treat upper-airway obstructions (or choking) by foreign objects. American doctor Henry Heimlich is often credited for its development. To perform a Heimlich maneuver, a rescuer stands behind a choking victim and uses their hands to apply pressure to the bottom of the victim's diaphragm. This compresses the lungs and exerts pressure on the object lodged in the trachea in an effort to expel it.
Most modern protocols, including those of the American Heart Association, American Red Cross, and European Resuscitation Council, recommend that treatment of airway obstructions be performed in several stages designed to apply increasing levels of pressure. Most protocols recommend encouraging the victim to cough, followed by hard back slaps, and finally abdominal thrusts…
