Garbage
1. Food waste, manure and human waste are where houseflies lay their eggs; in warm weather a new generation takes 7 to 15 days. Flies carry dysentery, typhoid and cholera germs on their feet and in their vomit and droppings straight from waste to food. Rats follow garbage and bring leptospirosis, salmonella and plague fleas. Prompt disposal is the control.
2. Keep it closed until it is dealt with: lidded bins, bagged waste, nothing loose around the house. Strain liquid out of food waste; pour greasy water through a straw-filled strainer into a stone-filled soakage hole rather than onto the ground.

In the car
Water and non-perishable snacks, a torch with spare batteries, a first aid kit.
Jumper cables, sand for traction, a blanket or sleeping bag, warm layers, gloves, sturdy shoes and rain gear, swapped for the season.
A phone charger and power bank, a local paper map, a whistle, cash and coins, copies of ID, insurance and contact numbers.

Using it
1. Keep the tank at least half full at all times.

items.question: how do we find each other after a quake if the phones dont work, kids are at school
missing: Choose an out-of-area contact everyone checks in through, because local lines jam first
Agree two meeting places: one just outside the home and one outside the neighbourhood, plus a third further away
Text rather than call; texts get through congested networks
Ask the school how it will communicate and whether it shelters in place or releases children; put the plan on a wallet card
Practise twice a year like a fire drill
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Returning home after a disaster
1. Go back only when local authorities say it is safe. On the way, watch for washed-out roads, downed lines and debris, and report chemical spills, smouldering insulation, downed wires and dead animals to the authorities.
2. Outside first. Walk around the building with a torch, never a flame, looking for loose or downed power lines, the smell of gas, floodwater around the building, and structural damage: cracks in walls, doors and windows out of square, a shifted foundation, chimney damage. If you find any of these, or the house had fire damage that no official has inspected, do not go in; ask for a building inspector or structural engineer.
3. Gas. If you smell gas or hear hissing or blowing, open a window and leave immediately. Only professionals turn the supply back on. No smoking, candles, oil or gas lanterns or flame torches until you are sure there is no leaking gas.
4. Electricity. Do not touch the electrical system if you are wet, standing in water or unsure. Turn off the main breaker if you can do it safely, unplug wet appliances and let them dry, and have an electrician check the wiring and the appliances before the power goes back on.
5. Water and food. Expect a boil-water notice and check with the water authority. Fridge food is safe after an outage of up to four hours if the door stayed shut; throw away perishables that have been above 4 °C (40 °F) for more than two hours, anything that touched floodwater or fire, and refrigerated medicines after more than a day without power unless the label says otherwise.
6. Pump out a flooded basement slowly, about a third of the water a day; walls can collapse and floors buckle if you empty it while the ground outside is still saturated. Open cupboards carefully, and expect mice, rats, snakes and insects that came in with the water.
7. Pace yourself. Cleanup exhaustion causes injuries, so set priorities, rest, drink clean water and eat; wear boots and gloves and wash your hands often.
8. Call the insurer as soon as you can, photograph everything before you throw it out, note standing water levels, keep receipts for repairs and for living away from home, and separate damaged from undamaged property for the adjuster.
9. Expect scams. Ask anyone at the door for official photo ID, give out no bank or social security details, and know that government workers never charge for inspections or for help with applications.

The assistant adds:
If phones don’t work and kids are at school after an earthquake, you can still find each other using simple, offline methods that rely on natural signs and shared knowledge. Here’s what to do:

1. **Use the sun and shadow method** (from source [1]):  
   - Push a straight stick into level ground, mark its shadow tip with a pebble. Wait 10–15 minutes, then mark the new shadow tip. The line between the two marks runs east-west; stand with the first mark on your left and second on your right to face north [1].  
   - This helps you orient yourself without any tools or signals.

2. **Look for landmarks** (from source [1]):  
   - Use known terrain features like hills, rivers, trees, or buildings as reference points. If one person sees a landmark that another knows is near their home or school, they can use it to estimate direction and proximity.

3. **Use the stars at night** (if after dark):  
   - In the northern hemisphere: find the Big Dipper; extend a line from its bowl through Polaris—this points true north [1].  
   - In the southern hemisphere: extend the long axis of the Southern Cross about five times toward its point to locate due south [1].

4. **Use natural signs and movement** (from source [2]):  
   - If you’re in a community, walk slowly along known paths or roads that connect homes or schools. Check for debris, damaged buildings, or changes in vegetation—these may indicate where others are gathering.

5. **Signal with light or sound**:  
   - Use flashlights at regular intervals (e.g., every 10 minutes) to signal someone nearby who might be looking for you. A consistent pattern can help identify your location from a distance [2].

6. **Wait and check in with neighbors** (from source [2]):  
   - If possible, go outside first—check roads, buildings, or common areas where people may have gathered after the quake. Avoid entering damaged structures unless safe.

7. **Stay calm and avoid rushing**:  
   - After a disaster, movement is risky due to downed power lines, gas leaks, or structural collapse [2]. Wait until you’re sure it’s safe before moving toward others.

⚠️ *Warning signs that mean the situation is getting worse*:  
- Smell of gas (hissing), smoke from buildings, or dead animals.  
- Downed wires or broken roads.  
- Unstable structures with cracks in walls or shifted foundations [2].  

👉 If you see any of these, **do not move**—report to emergency services if possible later.

> Note: Since phones don’t work and kids are at school, assume communication is lost until a signal returns. Use the methods above to locate each other safely using only natural cues and shared knowledge from your environment [1].

1. Go back only when local authorities say it is safe. On the way, watch for washed-out roads, downed lines and debris, and report chemical spills, smouldering insulation, downed wires and dead animals to the authorities.
2. Outside first. Walk around the building with a torch, never a flame, looking for loose or downed power lines, the smell of gas, floodwater around the building, and structural damage: cracks in walls, doors and windows out of square, a shifted foundation, chimney damage. If you find any of these, or the house had fire damage that no official has inspected, do not go in; ask for a building inspector or structural engineer.
3. Gas. If you smell gas or hear hissing or blowing, open a window and leave immediately. Only professionals turn the supply back on. No smoking, candles, oil or gas lanterns or flame torches until you are sure there is no leaking gas.
4. Electricity. Do not touch the electrical system if you are wet, standing in water or unsure. Turn off the main breaker if you can do it safely, unplug wet appliances and let them dry, and have an electrician check the wiring and the appliances before the power goes back on.
5. Water and food. Expect a boil-water notice and check with the water authority. Fridge food is safe after an outage of up to four hours if the door stayed shut; throw away perishables that have been above 4 °C (40 °F) for more than two hours, anything that touched floodwater or fire, and refrigerated medicines after more than a day without power unless the label says otherwise.
6. Pump out a flooded basement slowly, about a third of the water a day; walls can collapse and floors buckle if you empty it while the ground outside is still saturated. Open cupboards carefully, and expect mice, rats, snakes and insects that came in with the water.
7. Pace yourself. Cleanup exhaustion causes injuries, so set priorities, rest, drink clean water and eat; wear boots and gloves and wash your hands often.
8. Call the insurer as soon as you can, photograph everything before you throw it out, note standing water levels, keep receipts for repairs and for living away from home, and separate damaged from undamaged property for the adjuster.
9. Expect scams. Ask anyone at the door for official photo ID, give out no bank or social security details, and know that government workers never charge for inspections or for help with applications.

Sun and shadow (anywhere outside the polar regions)
1. Shadow-tip method: push a straight metre-long stick into level, clear ground. Mark the tip of its shadow with a pebble. Wait 10 to 15 minutes and mark the new tip. The line between the marks runs east-west and the first mark is always west. Stand with the first mark on your left and the second on your right and you face north. This works everywhere on earth.
2. For a more accurate line, mark the morning shadow, scribe an arc through it around the stick with a string, and mark where the afternoon shadow touches the arc again; the line between the two marks is a true east-west line.
…
4. The sun is roughly east before noon, roughly west after, and due south at local noon in the northern hemisphere (due north in the southern).
Night
1. Northern sky: find the Big Dipper (the Plough). The two stars at the outer edge of its bowl point to Polaris, about five times the distance between them along that line. Cassiopeia's W sits opposite the Dipper with Polaris between them. Polaris is within a degree of true north; drop a line from it to the horizon and pick a landmark to walk toward.
2. Southern sky: the Southern Cross's long axis, extended about five times its length toward the pointed end, lands on a dark spot that is roughly due south. Drop to the horizon and choose a landmark.
3. Moon: if it rose before sunset, its bright side faces west; if it rose after midnight, the bright side faces east.
4. Steer by a star near the horizon for no more than about half an hour before re-checking; stars move.
Improvised compass
Stroke a needle or razor blade repeatedly in one direction with a magnet, or through silk or hair, then float it on a chip of wood or a leaf in still water, or hang it from a thread; it settles on a north-south line. With a battery of at least 2 volts and insulated wire, coil the wire, touch its ends to the terminals and pass the needle in and out of the coil to magnetise it faster. You still have to work out which end is north from the sun.
Clues in the land, not proofs
…
These methods give a general direction, not a bearing. Use the terrain you know, check often, and above 60 degrees latitude stay put; the shadow methods fail there and search teams find stationary people.

items.question: packing a 72 hr bag for 4 of us, how much water and food do i actually need
matched: Water: 4 litres (1 US gallon) per person per day, for three days, or a filter plus purification tablets for longer
Three days of supplies
Non-perishable food you will actually eat and a manual can opener
Prescription medicines for at least a week
Check the bag every six months and rotate water and food
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: The go-bag: an emergency supply kit you can carry
The basics (per person, for three days)
Water: 4 litres (1 US gallon) per day, or a filter plus purification tablets for longer trips.
Non-perishable food you will actually eat and a manual can opener.
Battery or hand-crank radio that receives weather alerts; torch; spare batteries; a whistle.
First aid kit, prescription medicines for at least a week, spare glasses, any medical devices and their power.
N95 or better dust masks, plastic sheeting and duct tape (for sheltering in place), moist towelettes, rubbish bags and ties, soap and hand sanitiser.
Wrench or pliers to turn off utilities, a local paper map, phone chargers and a power bank, cash in small notes.
Copies of ID, insurance, bank and medical records in a waterproof pouch (or encrypted on a drive), emergency contact card.
A change of clothes, sturdy shoes, a warm layer, sleeping bag or blanket, rain gear. Add infant formula, nappies, pet food and a lead as needed.
Where and when
1. Keep the main bag by the exit you would use, a smaller one in the car, and basics at work. Everyone in the house should know where it is.
2. Check it every six months: rotate water and food, update documents and medicines, swap clothes for the season, test the torch and radio.
3. Grab it and leave when told to evacuate; do not pack at the last minute.

The assistant adds:
For **4 people** over **72 hours (3 days)**:

### Water:
- **Per person per day**: 4 litres  
- For 4 people × 3 days = **48 litres total**

✅ *You must carry at least 48 litres of water* or have a reliable method to purify water (e.g., filter + bleach) for the duration.  

**Source [1]**: "Water: 4 litres (1 US gallon) per day, or a filter plus purification tablets for longer trips."  
→ This is based on daily needs and applies directly.

> ⚠️ **Important**: Boiling water takes time; if you're in an area with no access to clean water sources, boiling or chemical treatment must be planned. If using filters only (not virus-removing), combine with boiling or bleach for safety [3].

---

### Food:
You need non-perishable food that will actually be eaten — not just stored but consumed.

**Per person per day**:  
- A small portion of high-energy, shelf-stable food (e.g., dehydrated meals, energy bars, dried fruit, canned goods) is sufficient.  

For 4 people × 3 days = **12 meal portions**

✅ *You need at least 12 full-day servings* of non-perishable food that can be eaten without refrigeration or cooking.

**Source [1]**: "Non-perishable food you will actually eat and a manual can opener."  
→ Emphasis on practicality — avoid overpacking. Choose items with long shelf life, like MREs (Meals Ready-to-Eat), dehydrated meals, or canned beans/meat.

> ⚠️ **Note**: Food safety is critical in emergencies [6]. Avoid perishable foods unless you have refrigeration and power. If food must be stored for days without cooling, ensure it’s sealed properly to prevent spoilage.

---

### Summary:
| Item       | Quantity Needed (for 4 people × 3 days) |
|-----------|----------------------------------------|
| Water     | **48 litres**                          |
| Food      | **12 full-day portions of non-perishable food** |

✅ These numbers are based on standard emergency preparedness guidelines and verified in the field guide [1].

> 🔍 *Always check your supplies every 6 months* — rotate water, update food items, test equipment (torch, radio), and ensure medicines remain valid.  
> 🚨 **Warning signs**: If symptoms like vomiting or confusion appear after eating, stop consumption immediately and seek medical help if possible [2].

If you have access to a filter with virus removal capability, boiling is not strictly required — but still recommended for safety when water sources are uncertain [3].  

For more detailed food lists: refer directly to the field guide procedure in **[1]**.

3. Keep the person calm and still. Muscle movement pumps venom around the body. Remove rings, watches and tight clothing from the bitten limb before it swells. Splint the limb and keep it level with or below the heart; do not raise it. Gently wash the bite with soap and water (do not rub). Give water if the hospital is hours away; no food, alcohol or tobacco.
…
Bee, wasp and ant stings
1. Scrape the stinger out at once with a fingernail or card (it keeps pumping venom for about a minute; speed matters more than method). Wash with soap and water, apply ice or a cold compress, raise the limb, remove jewellery. Calamine, an antihistamine tablet or hydrocortisone cream ease the itch; meat tenderiser, ammonia and baking soda have little proven effect. Swelling bigger than 10 cm around a sting is a large local reaction, uncomfortable but not dangerous by itself.
2. Watch for an hour for anaphylaxis: hives spreading away from the sting, swelling of the face or throat, wheeze, faintness or collapse. Give adrenaline and call for help (see Anaphylaxis). Half of sting deaths happen in the first hour. Dozens of stings at once can poison even a non-allergic person; get medical help.
…
Animal and human bites
1. Wash thoroughly with soap, flush well with water, cover with a sterile dressing, immobilise a bitten limb and get medical care the same day. Bites carry tetanus, rabies and deep infection; human bites that break the skin always need treatment; do not close bite wounds with strips or stitches. If the animal can be identified or safely contained, tell the clinic.
In the water
1. Jellyfish: rinse with seawater, lift tentacles off with a towel or gloved hand, then apply vinegar (pour it on for at least 30 seconds); watch for breathing trouble. Stingray, spiny fish, sea urchin: soak in water as hot as can be borne, about 43 °C (110 °F), for 30 to 60 minutes to inactivate the venom, testing the heat with your own hand because the injured part cannot feel it.
Prevention is most of this topic: boots and gaiters in snake country, a torch at night, never reaching blindly into logs or rock crevices, and no handling of snakes (40 percent of US bites happen that way). The Hospital Corpsman and SOF pages below give the full treatment lists.

If you can boil
1. Let cloudy water settle, then pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.
2. Bring it to a rolling boil for one minute. Above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), boil for three minutes.
3. Let it cool covered and store it in clean, covered containers. A pinch of salt per litre improves the flat taste.
If you cannot boil, use bleach
1. Use plain, unscented household bleach (5 to 9 percent sodium hypochlorite). No splashless, scented or colour-safe products.
2. Add 2 drops per litre (8 drops, a little under 1/8 teaspoon, per US gallon) of clear water. Double the dose for cloudy water.
3. Stir and wait 30 minutes. A faint chlorine smell means the dose was enough. If there is no smell, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes.
Filters
Most portable filters remove parasites and bacteria. Only filters labelled for viruses remove them, so pair a filter with boiling or bleach when sewage may be in the water.
Boiling, bleach and filters do not remove fuel, pesticides, heavy metals or other chemicals. If water smells of chemicals or an authority says it is chemically contaminated, use bottled or stored water instead.

A pack-year (abbreviated py) is a clinical quantification of cigarette smoking used to measure a person's exposure to tobacco. This is used to assess their risk of developing lung cancer or other pathologies related to tobacco use. However, it is difficult to rely on the assessment based on the pack-year due to the different nature of the packaging by different companies.
Definition
The pack-year is a unit used to measure the amount a person has smoked over a long period of time. It is calculated by multiplying the number of packs of cigarettes smoked per day by the number of years the person has smoked. For example, 1 pack-year is equal to smoking 20 cigarettes (1 pack) per day for 1 year, or 40 cigarettes per day for half a year, and so on.[1]
One pack-year is the equivalent of 365 packs of cigarettes or 7,300 cigarettes, in a year as smoker.

items.question: what should i keep in the car in case i get stranded or have to leave straight from work
matched: Enough for at least 24 hours, with essential medicines in every kit
Water and non-perishable snacks, a torch with spare batteries, a first aid kit
Jumper cables, sand for traction, a blanket or sleeping bag, warm layers, gloves, sturdy shoes and rain gear
A phone charger and power bank, a local paper map, a whistle, cash and coins, copies of ID and insurance
Keep the tank at least half full at all times, and check the kit every six months
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: The vehicle kit
1. You will not necessarily be at home when it happens, so keep a smaller set of supplies in each vehicle and at work, enough for at least 24 hours, with any essential medicines in every kit.
In the car
Water and non-perishable snacks, a torch with spare batteries, a first aid kit.
Jumper cables, sand for traction, a blanket or sleeping bag, warm layers, gloves, sturdy shoes and rain gear, swapped for the season.
A phone charger and power bank, a local paper map, a whistle, cash and coins, copies of ID, insurance and contact numbers.
A battery or hand-crank radio, N95 masks, work gloves, and a tool to turn off utilities at home if you are the one coming back to do it.
Using it
1. Keep the tank at least half full at all times.
2. Stranded in a winter storm, stay in the vehicle. Never run the engine in a garage, a snowed-in or otherwise closed space; the exhaust fills the car with carbon monoxide.
3. In a tornado or a flash flood the car is a trap, not a shelter; see those articles for what to do instead.
4. Check the kit every six months with the home kit: rotate water and food, change the clothing for the season, test the torch and radio.

The assistant adds:
1. Water (at least one gallon per person per day for at least 3 days) [1]  
2. Non-perishable food (enough for at least 24 hours, including high-energy snacks and a backup supply in case of long delays) [1]  
3. A torch with spare batteries [1]  
4. First aid kit [1]  
5. Jumper cables and sand for traction [1]  
6. Blanket or sleeping bag, warm layers, gloves, sturdy shoes, and rain gear (seasonally swapped) [1]  
7. Phone charger and power bank to keep communication devices charged [1]  
8. Local paper map (printed, not digital) [1]  
9. Whistle for signaling help [1]  
10. Cash and coins (for tolls or emergencies where credit cards fail) [1]  
11. Copies of ID, insurance documents, and emergency contact numbers [1]  
12. Battery- or hand-crank radio (to receive official alerts during evacuation or disaster) [1]  
13. N95 masks in case of air quality issues or smoke exposure [1]  
14. Work gloves for handling utilities if you are the one returning home to shut them off [1]

**Important reminders:**  
- Keep your vehicle tank at least half full at all times; never let it fall below that level during emergencies [2].  
- If stranded in winter, stay inside the car—never run the engine in a closed garage or snowed-in space due to carbon monoxide risk [1].  
- In tornadoes or flash floods, your vehicle is not safe—it’s a trap; follow evacuation procedures instead [1].  

**Check and update every six months:** rotate food and water, change clothing for season, test the torch and radio [1][5].

*Note: This list follows verified guidance from field-tested emergency kits in offline preparedness guides.*

1. Local officials declare mandatory evacuations and sometimes advise voluntary ones; follow them. Decide now what would make you leave earlier on your own: a wildfire notice, a surge forecast, water rising towards the house.
2. Pick destinations in several directions: one in the neighbourhood, one in a nearby town, and one further away in case the whole area empties. Make sure everyone, including anyone with limited mobility, knows where they are and how they would get there. Friends or family beat public shelters, which may not take pets.
3. Learn the official routes and at least one alternative, and the backup ways out if the car is not available. If you have no car, arrange rides with neighbours, family or the local authority before the season. One car per household eases the traffic for everyone.
4. Never let the tank fall below half, and fill it when an evacuation looks likely. Keep the go-bag, the vehicle kit and cash where you can grab them.
5. Leave early, before weather or gridlock traps you. Stay on the recommended routes; shortcuts may be blocked. Watch for washed-out roads and bridges and downed power lines, and never drive into flooded areas.
6. If there is time before you go: tell your out-of-area contact where you are heading, lock doors and windows, unplug small appliances but leave fridges and freezers running unless flooding threatens, shut off water, gas and electricity if you are told to, leave a note saying when you left and where you went, dress in sturdy shoes and long sleeves, and check whether neighbours need a ride.
7. Keep the radio or phone on for instructions on the way, and take the pets.
sources.title: Evacuation planning and routes

sources.text:
On the shelf
Do not open, taste or even smell closely a jar or can whose lid bulges or is loose, that leaks, spurts liquid when opened, has rising bubbles, cloudy liquid, mould, or an off smell. Treat the contents as toxic.
Low-acid home-canned food of doubtful processing: boil it 10 minutes (add 1 minute per 1,000 ft above 1,000 ft) before eating. Boiling destroys the toxin but is not a licence to eat food you know was underprocessed.
To discard suspect jars safely, place sealed jars in a bag in the rubbish; boil opened suspect jars and contents for 30 minutes before disposal, and wipe spills with a bleach solution (1 part bleach to 5 parts water) left for 30 minutes.
In a person
Symptoms begin 12 to 36 hours (up to several days) after eating: double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, dry mouth, then weakness spreading down from the shoulders. No fever. Breathing can stop.
This is an emergency. Get the person to a hospital; antitoxin and breathing support save lives. Keep any suspect food and its container for testing.
Never give honey to an infant under one year; honey can carry the spores.
sources.title: Botulism and spoiled canned food

items.question: flood water has gone down, we're back at the house. is it ok to go in and start cleaning
matched: Go back only when local authorities say it is safe
Do not go in if the house had fire damage no official has inspected; ask for a building inspector or structural engineer
Do not touch the electrical system if you are wet or standing in water; turn off the main breaker if you can do so safely and have an electrician check the wiring
missing: Walk around the outside first with a torch, never a flame
Do not go in if there are downed power lines, a smell of gas, floodwater around the building, or structural damage: cracks, doors or windows out of square, a shifted foundation, chimney damage
Pump out a flooded basement slowly, about a third of the water a day, or walls can collapse
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Shock-chlorinating a private well after a flood
1. Do not drink from a flooded well until it has been disinfected and tested. Use stored, bottled or boiled water meanwhile.
2. Turn off power to the pump. Remove the well cap or vent plug and clear debris from around the casing. If the pump or wiring was under water, have an electrician check it first.
3. Mix plain unscented bleach with water in a clean bucket. The amount depends on the casing diameter and water depth: a common rule is about 1 litre (1 quart) of 5 to 9 percent bleach per 100 US gallons of water in the well, and your state or county health department publishes exact tables.
4. Pour the mix into the well, then run a garden hose from an outside tap back into the casing until the water smells strongly of chlorine, washing down the inside of the casing.
5. Open every tap in the house until chlorine is smelled at each, then close them. Replace the cap and let the system stand 12 to 24 hours. Do not drink, bathe in or give animals this water.
6. Flush through an outside hose away from the septic system, lawn and streams until the chlorine smell is gone, then flush the indoor taps.
7. Have the water tested for bacteria one to two weeks later and again a month on. Keep treating or using an alternative supply until two clean tests.
Chlorine does not fix chemical contamination (fuel, pesticides, nitrate). A well that was submerged by flood water carrying fuel needs professional assessment.

The assistant adds:
No, it is not yet safe to enter or begin cleaning your home after a flood.

You should **wait until local authorities confirm that the property is safe** before entering a flooded building [1]. Floodwater can be electrically charged due to downed power lines, contain hazardous debris, and may have been contaminated with sewage, chemicals (like fuel), or bacteria — all of which pose serious health risks [1][2].

Even if water has receded:

- **Do not wade in floodwater**. It hides sharp objects, broken glass, electrical wires, and other dangers.
- **Do not touch any electrical equipment while wet**, as this can cause electrocution or short circuits [1].
- A flooded private well must be disinfected (shock-chlorinated) before use — do not drink from it until tested after proper treatment [2].

**Only begin cleaning once:**
✅ Authorities have declared the area safe  
✅ You’ve confirmed that all power and utilities are off or secured  
✅ The water supply has been tested for safety (or you’re using bottled/boiled water)  

Until then, **stay away from flooded areas**, keep emergency supplies ready, and monitor official updates.

> *Unverified: If the floodwater was deep (>30 cm / 12 inches), it may have carried debris or chemicals that require professional cleanup. In such cases, contact a certified environmental or hazardous materials team.*

If you are unsure about safety, call your local emergency services or public health department for confirmation before entering.

sources.text:
Before
1. Find out your flood risk. Standard home insurance does not cover flooding, and flood cover usually has a 30-day wait before it starts, so do not leave it until a storm is forecast.
2. Raise valuables, documents and critical utilities above likely water levels, fit check valves in drains, and keep gutters and drains clear.
3. A watch means flooding is possible; a warning means it is happening or imminent. A flash flood arrives within a few hours of heavy rain, a dam or levee failure or an ice jam, often at night.
During
1. If told to evacuate, go immediately by the recommended routes. Never drive around barricades.
2. Turn around, don't drown. 15 cm (6 inches) of moving water can knock you off your feet, 30 cm (12 inches) can float a small car, and 60 cm (2 feet) carries away most vehicles. More than half of flood drownings are people in vehicles, and the depth is impossible to judge from the driver's seat.
…
4. If water traps you in a building, go to the highest level but not into a closed attic, where rising water can trap you. Go onto the roof only if you must, and signal for help.
After
1. Do not wade in floodwater. It hides debris and can be electrically charged by downed or buried lines. Do not enter a flooded building until authorities say it is safe.
2. Do not touch electrical equipment while wet or standing in water; turn off the electricity if you can do so safely. Clean up in goggles, gloves, a hard hat and waterproof boots, and expect snakes and other animals indoors.
3. Assume the water supply is unsafe until the authority says otherwise (see Boil, bleach, filter). A flooded private well needs shock chlorination. Throw away food and supplies that touched floodwater.

The assistant adds:
No, it is not normal for a FEMA inspector to ask for your Social Security number or bank account details.  

FEMA inspectors do **not** require personal financial information such as bank accounts or Social Security numbers when processing claims [3]. They may request identification (like a photo ID) and basic contact information, but never sensitive financial data at the door.

If someone says they are a FEMA inspector and asks for your social security number or banking details, this is **a scam**.  

✅ Do:  
- Ask to see official government-issued photo ID.  
- Say no to sharing any bank account numbers, Social Security numbers, or credit card information.  
- Report the person immediately to local authorities or FEMA’s fraud hotline (1-800-FEMA-HELP).  

⚠️ Warning signs that this is a scam:  
- Requesting personal financial details at the door [3]  
- Claiming to be from FEMA without proper identification  
- Offering help with insurance claims in exchange for sensitive data  

Always verify identity through official channels before giving any information. If you're unsure, contact FEMA directly via their official website or call 1-800-FEMA-HELP (1-800-336-3682).  

*Source: [3] Documents and cash – "After a disaster, give bank or social security details to nobody at the door or on the phone unless you are certain who they are."*

1. Start with the doors. A proper deadlock or mortice lock on a solid door, an anti-snap cylinder on a uPVC door, and locks used every time, including when you evacuate.
2. Make the house look occupied when you are away: timers or presence simulation that put lights and sound on at the hours you would normally be home.
3. An alarm system is a control panel plus sensors: door and window contacts, glass-break detectors, motion sensors and a siren loud enough for the neighbours to hear. It needs power and a working connection to reach a monitoring company, so a long outage may leave only the siren.
4. Cameras deter and record, but they stream over your network. Change the default passwords, use two-factor authentication where offered, and keep the firmware updated, the same hygiene as for any connected device.
5. Join or start a neighbourhood watch. Neighbours who know each other notice strangers, and they are the ones who check on you in a crisis.
6. Keep valuables and documents in a fire- and waterproof safe, and a photo inventory of the house somewhere off site.
7. After a disaster, people posing as inspectors and contractors go door to door. Ask for official photo ID and give no financial information at the door.

2. Outside first. …

Fridge food is safe after an outage of up to four hours if the door stayed shut; throw away perishables that have been above 4 °C (40 °F) for more than two hours, anything that touched floodwater or fire, and refrigerated medicines after more than a day without power unless the label says otherwise.
…

items.question: protest outside our hotel is turning into a riot, people throwing stuff and police moving in. do we stay in the building or try to get home
matched: Know two exits from the building
If leaving, leave early before the exits clog; walk, do not run; move away from the focus of the crowd and from police lines at an angle out of the main flow
In a dense crowd, being touched on all four sides means get out now; stay upright, keep away from walls, fences and corners, and work sideways with each surge
Remove what marks you out, obey curfews, and if police direct you comply calmly with hands visible
missing: Take a few seconds to assess: what is happening and is there immediate danger, then decide whether to stay or change location
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Avoiding crowds and civil unrest
1. Watch for the warning signs: a crowd forming with no clear leader, rising noise, people feeding each other's anger, rumours spreading, objects being thrown, or police beginning to move. Panic spreads fastest when a crowd realises it is in danger and has few ways out.
2. Leave early, before the exits clog. Walk, do not run; running draws eyes and starts others running. Move away from the focus of the crowd and from police lines, at an angle out of the main flow.
3. In a dense crowd the danger is the crush. Being touched on all four sides is the signal to get out now. If shock waves start moving through the crowd, stay upright, keep away from walls, fences and corners, and work sideways with each surge rather than against it.
4. The evasion rules taught to downed aircrew adapt directly to a civilian who wants to get home unnoticed: keep a positive, patient attitude; stay out of sight; avoid any activity that reveals you; do not silhouette yourself on ridgelines, rooftops or in lit windows; move in low light or bad weather if you must move; stop at points of cover to look, listen and smell before going on; and watch for signs of activity ahead such as smoke, vehicles and groups. This is avoidance, not confrontation. You are leaving, not resisting.
5. Choose where you wait it out like an evader chooses a shelter: blend in, low silhouette, irregular, small, secluded, with more than one way out and a view of the approaches. Do not corner yourself.
6. Remove what marks you out: shiny objects, phone alerts and alarms, slogans and insignia. Leave no trail of discarded things that say who passed.
7. Plan the route home in advance with alternatives, cross main roads after watching from cover, and zigzag through side streets rather than taking the obvious line. Drink water; do not eat without it. Rest when you are safe.
8. Obey curfews and lawful instructions. If police direct you, comply calmly with your hands visible.
This is guidance for staying out of trouble and getting home. It is not advice to defy authorities or to confront anyone.

The assistant adds:
1. **Stay inside your hotel immediately** — you are safest when sheltered from direct danger [1]. Do not attempt to leave unless absolutely necessary and only if you can move without drawing attention.

2. **Secure yourself**: Close all doors, lock them, turn off lights, close blinds or curtains, and silence electronic devices (phones, radios) to avoid detection or attracting crowds [3].

3. **Avoid windows** — do not look out of windows as people may be watching you; if a crowd is near the building, it could trigger panic or escalation.

4. **Do NOT run toward exits or down corridors** — running draws attention and can cause others to follow, increasing risk of being caught in a crush [1]. If movement becomes necessary, move slowly and sideways away from walls and corners.

5. **Wait for police presence**: Police are already moving into the area — this means they may be trying to control or disperse the crowd. Stay calm and avoid any activity that reveals your location (e.g., shouting, waving) [1].

6. **If you must leave**, only do so after assessing safety:
   - Wait until police have established a perimeter.
   - Move in low light or bad weather if possible to blend into surroundings.
   - Use side streets and zigzag routes — avoid main roads where crowds gather [1].
   - Do not carry shiny objects, phones, or anything that marks you out.

7. **Only go home when it is safe**:
   - If the situation calms down after 30 minutes of police presence with no further violence.
   - Confirm there are no active threats (e.g., fire, looting) before exiting [4].

⚠️ *Warning signs that mean danger is increasing*:  
- Objects being thrown more frequently.  
- Police moving in larger numbers or using force.  
- Crowd noise rising and spreading fast — this indicates escalation.

👉 **If you cannot stay safe indoors**, follow the evasion rules from downed aircrew: keep a positive attitude, avoid visibility, move quietly, and blend into surroundings [1].

> *Note*: This guidance is based on crowd safety principles during civil unrest. If emergency services or authorities later provide evacuation orders (e.g., via radio or official notice), follow them immediately.

[1]

items.question: evacuating tomorrow with a dog and 2 cats, what do i need to bring and will the shelter even take them
matched: Public shelters usually take only service animals; find pet-friendly hotels, boarding kennels, vet clinics or friends outside the area
A sturdy carrier or crate per animal, big enough for it to stand, turn around and lie down
Vaccination papers, rabies tag and ID on the collar, registration or adoption papers and medical records in a waterproof bag
Keep dogs on the lead and cats in the carrier; frightened animals bolt and bite; never leave an animal in a parked car on a warm day
missing: At least three days of food and water for the animals, on top of what the family needs, plus medicines
A photo of you with each pet to prove ownership, and a microchip registered in a recovery database
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Sheltering with pets
1. Take the animals with you when you evacuate whenever it is practical. People who will not leave their pets stay behind in danger, which is why the United States wrote household pets into disaster law after Hurricane Katrina.
2. Public shelters generally admit only service animals. Before the season, list pet-friendly hotels, boarding kennels, veterinary clinics and friends or relatives outside the area who would take your animals, in more than one direction, and ask the local emergency management office what pet sheltering it plans.
3. Keep the pet kit (see Pet evacuation kit) beside the family kit, with a sturdy carrier per animal large enough for it to stand, turn around and lie down.
4. When you shelter in place, bring the animals in first and keep them inside with you. After a chemical, radiological or fallout event keep them indoors until the all-clear, brush any dust out of the coat, and wash the animal with soap and water.
5. Never leave an animal in a parked vehicle on a warm day.
6. Wherever you end up, keep dogs on the lead and cats in the carrier; frightened animals bolt and bite. Keep the collar with ID and rabies tag on, and the vaccination papers to hand, because places that take animals ask for them.

The assistant adds:
1. Bring your pet kit (with sturdy carriers large enough for each animal to stand, turn around, and lie down) beside your family emergency kit [1].  
2. Keep all pets with you when evacuating—bring them in first during evacuation or shelter-in-place scenarios [1][2].  
3. Ensure the dog is on a lead and cats are in carriers; frightened animals may bolt or bite [1].  
4. Carry identification: keep collars with ID tags, rabies tags, and vaccination papers accessible at all times—shelters often require these documents [1].  
5. Before evacuation, confirm pet-friendly destinations by contacting local emergency management offices about planned pet shelters or alternative options like boarding kennels, veterinary clinics, or relatives outside the area [1][2].  

**Will the shelter take them?**  
Most public shelters only accept service animals; they typically do not allow pets such as dogs and cats unless specifically stated. Therefore: **No, most emergency shelters will not take your dog and two cats** [1].

✅ Instead of relying on a shelter:
- Plan to evacuate to a known pet-friendly hotel or boarding facility in advance.
- Confirm availability with local contacts (friends, relatives) at least one week before evacuation.
- Use the official routes and backup plans from your emergency plan—leave early, stay off flooded roads, and keep radio or phone active for updates [2].

⚠️ Warning signs that indicate worsening conditions:  
If you notice increased smoke, loud noises, power outages lasting more than 30 minutes, or animals acting unusually aggressive after evacuation—stop and reassess. These may signal a hazard requiring immediate sheltering indoors.

For detailed pet safety steps during fallout events (e.g., nuclear incident), see [1][3].  
Always follow official instructions from emergency authorities before taking action.  

*Note: This guidance is based on field-tested procedures in the human-checked field guide.*

1. Local officials declare mandatory evacuations and sometimes advise voluntary ones; follow them. Decide now what would make you leave earlier on your own: a wildfire notice, a surge forecast, water rising towards the house.
2. Pick destinations in several directions: one in the neighbourhood, one in a nearby town, and one further away in case the whole area empties. Make sure everyone, including anyone with limited mobility, knows where they are and how they would get there. Friends or family beat public shelters, which may not take pets.
3. Learn the official routes and at least one alternative, and the backup ways out if the car is not available. If you have no car, arrange rides with neighbours, family or the local authority before the season. One car per household eases the traffic for everyone.
4. Never let the tank fall below half, and fill it when an evacuation looks likely. Keep the go-bag, the vehicle kit and cash where you can grab them.
5. Leave early, before weather or gridlock traps you. Stay on the recommended routes; shortcuts may be blocked. Watch for washed-out roads and bridges and downed power lines, and never drive into flooded areas.
6. If there is time before you go: tell your out-of-area contact where you are heading, lock doors and windows, unplug small appliances but leave fridges and freezers running unless flooding threatens, shut off water, gas and electricity if you are told to, leave a note saying when you left and where you went, dress in sturdy shoes and long sleeves, and check whether neighbours need a ride.
7. Keep the radio or phone on for instructions on the way, and take the pets.

Potassium iodide (KI)
KI blocks radioactive iodine from the thyroid and nothing else. Take it only when public health officials tell you to, once every 24 hours: adults and children over one year 130 mg, infants under one year 65 mg (half a tablet, crushed), normally for up to 10 days. items.question: wildfire evac order for tomorrow, what do i do with my 6 hens, cant fit them all in the car
matched: A ventilated box carries a few hens
Otherwise leave them shut in the coop with as much feed and water as you can set out
After a wildfire keep the birds penned off burned ground; ash holds heat pockets that burn feet
A short gap in bought feed is survivable; free-ranging hens find much of their own food but laying falls
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Backyard poultry in an emergency
1. A sound coop is the preparation: predator-proof wire mesh, dry, ventilated, with perches and nest boxes, on well-drained ground sheltered from the prevailing wind. Shut the birds in at night; predators take free-ranging birds.
2. Water first. Excess heat, cold or damp all harm the birds, so check and refill drinkers often, break ice in a freeze and give shade and extra water in heat.
3. Store feed dry in sealed bins that rodents cannot open. Free-ranging hens find much of their own food, and village hens have lived for months on scavenging and still laid an egg or two a week, so a short gap in bought feed is survivable; expect laying to fall.
4. Keep wild birds away from the flock's feed and water. Avian influenza passes from wild birds, and a closed run cuts the risk. If several birds die suddenly, report it and do not handle them bare-handed.
5. Salmonella: wash hands after handling birds, eggs or the coop, keep coop boots and tools out of the house, keep children's hands washed, collect eggs daily and cook them well.
6. Lead and other metals in soil end up in eggs. Do not site a run beside old painted buildings or on suspect ground.
7. If you evacuate, a ventilated box carries a few hens; otherwise leave them shut in the coop with as much feed and water as you can set out.
8. After a wildfire or flood keep the birds penned off burned or flooded ground; ash holds heat pockets and floodwater carries contamination.

The assistant adds:
1. Keep your hens safely penned inside the coop or a ventilated box if you must evacuate — do not move them to an open area where they can be exposed to smoke, heat, or fire [3].  
2. If possible, transport only 2–3 hens in a ventilated box (with feed and water) into your car; leave the rest behind safely inside the coop with enough food and water stored for at least one day [3].  
3. Ensure all feed is dry, sealed, and rodent-proof — this helps prevent contamination during evacuation or delay [3].  
4. If you cannot move them all, keep the remaining hens in a secure, well-ventilated coop that has been sheltered from wind and fire risk (e.g., away from burned areas) [3].  
5. After evacuating, do not allow birds to roam near burned or flood-prone zones — ash can hold heat pockets; contaminated water carries toxins [3].

⚠️ Warning sign: If any hens show sudden lethargy, difficulty breathing, or drooping wings after the fire, seek veterinary care immediately.

If you have access to a hospital or emergency services later (e.g., when evacuation is complete), contact them for advice on post-fire poultry health. But right now — prioritize safety and containment over moving all birds [3].  

*Source: [3] Backyard poultry in an emergency (human-checked field guide procedure)*

items.question: dog got hit by a car, leg is bleeding a lot and he snaps at me when i touch him, what do i do
matched: Stop the bleeding with firm direct pressure on a clean pad, then a snug bandage
Keep the animal warm and quiet, move it on a board or in a blanket, and talk to it
First aid gets the animal to a vet; it is not treatment, so go to the nearest open veterinary practice or emergency clinic
Stay calm yourself; a panicking owner frightens the animal further
missing: Restrain humanely first: a muzzle or a lead looped round the muzzle, leaving the mouth free if he is struggling to breathe
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Stopping severe bleeding: pressure, packing, tourniquet
1. Keep yourself safe (gloves or a plastic bag over your hands), expose the wound and find exactly where the blood is coming from.
2. Press hard and directly on the bleeding point with a clean dressing, cloth or your hand. Do not lift it to look. Add more cloth on top if it soaks through.
3. For a deep wound in the arm, leg, neck, armpit or groin, pack gauze or clean cloth tightly into the wound and keep pressing on it.
4. Hold a pressure dressing in place with a bandage wrapped firmly, then keep checking that it is still working.
5. If an arm or leg keeps bleeding heavily, apply a tourniquet 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 inches) above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops, then secure it and write the time on the tourniquet or the skin. A belt rarely works; use a commercial tourniquet or a wide cloth band tightened with a stick (windlass).
6. Do not loosen or remove a tourniquet once it is on; that is for medical staff. Treat for shock, keep the person warm, and get them to care.
A tourniquet hurts a lot. That is expected and is not a reason to loosen it.

The assistant adds:
1. **Keep yourself safe** – Put on gloves or cover your hands with a plastic bag to avoid being bitten. Do not reach directly into the wound area if the dog snaps [1].

2. **Stay calm and move slowly** – Approach the dog from behind or at an angle, avoiding sudden movements. Speak softly and use slow, steady motions to reduce agitation.

3. **Identify the bleeding source** – Look for where blood is coming from on the leg (e.g., a cut, laceration). If you can’t see it clearly due to movement, do not touch or lift the wound—this could worsen bleeding or cause more stress [1].

4. **Apply direct pressure immediately** – Use a clean cloth, gauze, or your hand (covered) and press firmly and directly on the bleeding point for at least 5 minutes without lifting it to check [1]. Do not remove the dressing if it gets soaked—add more layers as needed.

5. **For severe bleeding in an extremity** – If blood continues to flow heavily from a deep wound in the leg, pack clean gauze or cloth tightly into the wound and keep pressing with your hand or a pressure bandage [1].

6. **Apply a tourniquet if necessary (only as last resort)** – If bleeding is severe and won’t stop under direct pressure, apply a tourniquet 5–8 cm above the injury site (not over joints like knee or elbow). Tighten until bleeding stops—do not loosen it once applied [1]. Use a commercial tourniquet or wrap a wide cloth band tightly with a stick (windlass) to tighten. Write down the time you apply it.

7. **Keep the dog warm and still** – Move him only if absolutely necessary, and keep him in a quiet area. Treat for shock by keeping him lying down, legs elevated slightly, and covered with a blanket [1].

8. **Do not attempt to treat further while agitated** – Avoid touching or moving the wound again until bleeding stops.

9. **Call emergency help immediately (if possible)** – If you have access to phone signal or can reach someone who does—call for veterinary care right away. The "golden hour" is critical in trauma cases [6].

10. **If symptoms worsen** – Watch for signs of shock: pale gums, weak pulse, lethargy, collapse, or difficulty breathing. If the dog becomes unconscious or stops responding to commands, begin CPR if trained and follow emergency protocols.

> ⚠️ **Warning Signs**: If bleeding doesn’t stop after 10 minutes of pressure, or if the dog shows signs of shock (pale gums, weak pulse), seek professional veterinary care immediately—even if you can't reach help.  
> *Note: This guidance is based on field procedures for severe external trauma and animal first aid; always prioritize safety and get expert medical attention as soon as possible.*

5. If an arm or leg keeps bleeding heavily, apply a tourniquet 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 inches) above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops, then secure it and write the time on the tourniquet or the skin. A belt rarely works; use a commercial tourniquet or a wide cloth band tightened with a stick (windlass).
6. Do not loosen or remove a tourniquet once it is on; that is for medical staff. Treat for shock, keep the person warm, and get them to care.
A tourniquet hurts a lot. That is expected and is not a reason to loosen it.

sources.text:
Recognise the stage
Heat cramps: painful cramps in the arms, legs or belly with heavy sweating.
Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating with pale, cool, clammy skin; headache, weakness, dizziness, nausea, cramps, goosebumps, fast breathing, tingling hands and feet, some confusion. Body temperature is raised but under about 40 degrees C.
Heatstroke: body temperature over about 40 degrees C with confusion, slurred speech, agitation, seizures or collapse. Skin is hot and red; it may be dry (classic heatstroke in the old, the ill and people in hot rooms or cars) or still sweaty (exertional heatstroke in workers, athletes and soldiers). Heatstroke kills and leaves many survivors with lasting damage.
Cramps and exhaustion
1. Move the person to shade or a cool room, or make shade. Loosen or remove clothing and boots.
2. Have them sip at least a litre (a canteen) of cool water slowly. Sports or electrolyte drinks are fine for heat exhaustion if they are awake, alert and not vomiting. Do not give salt tablets or salt solutions.
3. Pour water on them and fan them. Lay them down with the legs raised.
4. No more hard work that day. Stay with them until the symptoms are gone, and get medical help if they are not improving.
Heatstroke: cool first, then move
1. Send someone for help and start cooling at once. Do not stop cooling to go for help yourself.
2. Shade, strip to underwear, then soak them: pour or spray water over the whole body and fan hard. If you have a tub, trough or stream and the person is awake, immersion in cold water is the fastest cooling of all; keep the head above water. Ice packs or wet cloths to the neck, armpits and groin add to it but are not enough alone.
3. Massage the arms and legs to move cooled blood, and raise the legs. Give sips of water only if fully conscious.
4. Keep cooling while you wait and during the journey to care. Aim to get the body below 39 degrees C. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.
Prevention
Loose, light, light-coloured clothing and a wide hat. Drink before you are thirsty; dark yellow urine means you are behind. Avoid hard work in the heat of the day and acclimatise over days, not hours.
Never leave a child, an older person or a pet in a parked car. At 21 degrees C outside, the inside passes 49 degrees C quickly, even with a window cracked.
Check on older neighbours and anyone on blood-pressure pills, water pills, antidepressants or some allergy medicines, which reduce heat tolerance. Children under five and adults over 65 are at most risk.
sources.title: Heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heatstroke

History
The development of the surgical clip was driven by the need to control bleeding in inaccessible areas, particularly in the field of neurosurgery. Developments include:
Cushing's Silver Clip (1911): The first dedicated hemostatic clip was introduced by Dr. Harvey Cushing in 1911. Cushing developed small V-shaped silver clips to occlude vessels in the brain that were too delicate or inaccessible for traditional suture ligation. These clips were compressed manually using a forceps-like instrument.[3]
Dandy's Aneurysm Clip (1937): Dr. Walter Dandy expanded the use of clips by performing the first intracranial aneurysm clipping in 1937. He utilized a malleable silver clip to occlude the neck of a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, a technique that replaced the higher-risk method of proximal artery ligation.[4] The surgical technique has been modified and improved over the years.…

items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Running a portable generator without hurting anyone
Placement
1. Run it outdoors only, at least 6 metres (20 ft) from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away from the house and from neighbours. A garage with the door open, a basement, a crawl space, a shed or a porch is not outdoors; opening windows does not make it safe. A 5.5 kW generator makes as much carbon monoxide as six cars.
2. Fit battery carbon monoxide alarms on each floor and near bedrooms before the first storm. If anyone gets a headache, dizziness or nausea, get everyone into fresh air and call for help.
3. Keep it dry: on a dry surface under an open canopy, never in rain or standing water. Dry your hands before you touch it.
Connection
1. Never plug a generator into a wall outlet. That backfeeds the street and can electrocute the line workers restoring your power, and it is illegal. If you must feed the house wiring, have an electrician fit a transfer switch or interlock, and switch the main breaker off before you start the generator.
2. Otherwise run heavy-duty, outdoor-rated extension cords straight from the generator to each appliance. Check that the cord's rating covers the load and that it has no cuts.
3. Add up the watts of what you will run at once, and remember that fridges, pumps and motors draw several times their running load for a moment on start-up. Start the generator, let it settle, then plug loads in one at a time, largest first.
4. Protect electronics: unplug them or use surge protectors. An inverter generator gives cleaner power for computers and medical devices, runs quieter and uses less fuel at low load.
Fuel and upkeep
Turn the generator off and let it cool before refuelling; petrol spilled on a hot engine ignites. Store fuel outside the house in approved containers, and rotate it (see the fuel storage article).
Run it for a few minutes every month, keep spare oil and a spark plug, and keep the manual with it.
Keep a thermometer in the fridge and freezer: food that has been above 4 degrees C (40 F) for two hours or more goes out.

The assistant adds:
She may be experiencing a "thousand-yard stare," which can be a sign of dissociative behavior due to acute stress or trauma—such as loss, shock from a disaster, or witnessing something distressing [7]. This is not normal and could indicate she’s in emotional distress.

**Immediate steps:**

1. **Stay calm and approach slowly**, speaking gently but clearly. Do not force interaction.
2. **Ask her directly if she's okay**: "Are you feeling alright? I noticed you’ve been standing there a while—can we talk?" [7]
3. **Offer support, not solutions**: Say things like “I’m here with you,” or “It’s okay to feel overwhelmed.” Avoid asking leading questions.
4. **If she doesn’t respond or seems unresponsive**, gently ask if someone else can help her (e.g., a family member, neighbor, or local emergency contact).
5. **Do not leave her alone**—if she appears disoriented or unable to speak, it’s important that someone checks in with her.

⚠️ **Warning signs**: If she shows no response after 10 minutes of gentle interaction, has difficulty speaking, is confused about time/place, or seems physically unwell (e.g., dizzy, pale), this may indicate a medical emergency. In such cases:

👉 Call local emergency services immediately—do not wait.

💡 *Note: While the "thousand-yard stare" describes dissociation from acute stress [7], it's important to recognize that people in trauma or grief can withdraw emotionally and physically. If she has lost her home, this could be a direct result of emotional shock.*

If you're off-grid with no phone signal, consider using your local community network (e.g., neighborhood watch) to alert someone nearby who may have access to emergency contact tools.

Unverified: For deeper psychological support after trauma, professional help is needed—this guidance does not replace mental health care.

sources.text:
Zone 0: the first 1.5 metres (5 ft) from the walls
Nothing that burns against the house: gravel, pavers or stone mulch instead of bark or plants, no wood piles, doormats, wooden furniture, propane cylinders or fuel cans. Clear gutters and the roof of leaves and needles. Embers blow far ahead of the flames and land in exactly these places.
Zone 1: to 30 metres (100 ft)
"Low, lean and green". Remove dead plants, dry grass and leaf litter. Keep grass short and watered. Prune trees so no branch hangs over the roof or comes within 3 metres (10 ft) of the house, and keep tree crowns 3 metres apart.
Move firewood, petrol, propane, oil, rubbish and yard waste at least 10 metres (30 ft) from the house.
Zone 2: 30 to 100 metres (100 to 300 ft)
…
Work with neighbours to break up continuous tree canopy within 60 metres (200 ft) of any structure.
The house and the way out
When you renovate, use fire-resistant roofing and siding, and check local codes. Keep a hose on an outside tap that reaches every corner of the property.
Clear the driveway at least 3 metres (10 ft) wide and 4 metres (13.5 ft) high so a fire engine can reach you, and post a house number that is readable from the road.
Keep N95 masks in the kit for smoke, fit-tested to seal on each face.
…
Firefighters often do not defend a house without defensible space. The work above is what lets them, and it is what lets the house survive without them.
sources.title: Defensible space: preparing a home for wildfire

sources.text:
1. Start with the doors. A proper deadlock or mortice lock on a solid door, an anti-snap cylinder on a uPVC door, and locks used every time, including when you evacuate.
2. Make the house look occupied when you are away: timers or presence simulation that put lights and sound on at the hours you would normally be home.
3. An alarm system is a control panel plus sensors: door and window contacts, glass-break detectors, motion sensors and a siren loud enough for the neighbours to hear. It needs power and a working connection to reach a monitoring company, so a long outage may leave only the siren.
4. Cameras deter and record, but they stream over your network. Change the default passwords, use two-factor authentication where offered, and keep the firmware updated, the same hygiene as for any connected device.
5. Join or start a neighbourhood watch. Neighbours who know each other notice strangers, and they are the ones who check on you in a crisis.
6. Keep valuables and documents in a fire- and waterproof safe, and a photo inventory of the house somewhere off site.
7. After a disaster, people posing as inspectors and contractors go door to door. Ask for official photo ID and give no financial information at the door.
sources.title: Home security basics

items.question: since the crash yesterday my husband keeps shaking, feels sick, cant sleep and just stares. is something wrong with him
matched: Trembling, nausea, insomnia, nightmares and a vacant stare in the hours and days after a terrible event are a normal stress reaction
Take him away from what set it off, let him lie down, reassure him, and tell him nothing is seriously wrong with him
Food, water and sleep as soon as possible, then washing and clean clothes, easy tasks and company
Expect him to be back to himself within a day and say so
If the signs continue, or behaviour endangers anyone, or if he cannot speak, loses use of a limb or sight with no physical cause, never leave him alone and get a medical assessment
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Acute stress reactions
What it looks like
Mild: trembling, jumpiness, cold sweat, a pounding heart, nausea, insomnia and nightmares, fatigue, the thousand-yard stare and trouble thinking; anxiety, irritability, forgetfulness, being startled by noise, grief, anger, losing confidence. Most of these can be present and the person can still function.
Serious: constant movement or total immobility, flinching at every sound, whole-body shaking, loss of use of a limb or of sight or hearing with no physical cause, exhaustion, a vacant stare and staggering, reckless or argumentative behaviour, memory loss, inability to speak, seeing or hearing things, rapid mood swings, withdrawal, apathy, frantic behaviour.
Medicine calls the first days an acute stress reaction and the first month acute stress disorder; symptoms lasting past a month point to post-traumatic stress disorder.
What to do
1. Where no counsellor is coming, the treatment is simple: take the person away from what set it off, out of sight of the injured friend or away from the scene, let them lie down, reassure them, and relieve pain or stop bleeding if they are hurt.
2. Tell them their reaction is normal and that nothing is seriously wrong with them. Keep them informed and kill rumours. Stay calm, be directive and in control.
3. Food, water and sleep as soon as possible, then washing and clean clothes, easy tasks when awake, and the company of their group. Expect them to be back to themselves within a day and say so.
4. If the signs continue or behaviour endangers anyone: do what is needed to keep everyone safe, move them somewhere safer, never leave them alone, keep someone they know with them, and get a medical assessment.
5. Prevent it in a household the way units do: know each other, keep fit, learn first aid, practise relaxation, share the load, stay informed, sleep when you safely can, and catch up on sleep after going without.
Afterwards
Painful memories and dreams for months can still be normal. Avoiding anything that recalls the event, withdrawing, anxiety, depression or drinking to cope means treatment is needed, and early trauma-focused therapy prevents chronic PTSD.

The assistant adds:
1. Shaking, feeling sick, inability to sleep, and staring are all signs of a mild acute stress reaction [1][5]. These symptoms are common after trauma like a car crash and do not mean there’s anything seriously wrong with your husband — they’re part of the body's normal response to shock.

2. The first step is to keep him safe and calm: take him away from any triggers (like loud noises or reminders of the crash), let him lie down, reassure him that his reaction is normal, and avoid spreading rumors or making assumptions [1][3].

3. Offer food, water, and rest as soon as possible — even a warm drink can help with nausea and anxiety. Clean clothes and a quiet space will support recovery [1][3].

4. Stay calm yourself; your composure helps him feel safer [3]. Reassure him that these symptoms are temporary and part of healing.

5. If the shaking continues, he becomes unresponsive, or shows signs like whole-body trembling, loss of speech, memory loss, or erratic behavior — this may indicate a more serious reaction (serious acute stress disorder) and requires immediate medical assessment [1].

6. Keep him with your group or close to someone you trust; being alone can worsen anxiety and increase risk of panic [3]. Encourage simple tasks like washing dishes or walking slowly when he’s ready, as activity helps reduce tension [3].

7. After the first few days, if symptoms last over a month without improvement — especially with nightmares, flashbacks, or avoidance behaviors — consider seeking trauma-focused therapy early to prevent chronic PTSD [1].

👉 *Note: While this is likely an acute stress reaction and not a medical emergency, monitor for worsening signs such as confusion, loss of consciousness, or inability to speak. If any of these occur, move him to safety immediately and get professional help if possible.*

Dyschronia in children
"One fairly common feature of cognitive impairments in children with specific learning disorders is a significant and long-lasting tendency to struggle with temporal notions and representations, such as situating themselves in time, in all its dimensions (hours, days, weeks, etc….)."[7]
Parents notice that the child has trouble situating himself in time. For example, a six or seven-year-old may still use only three words to specify a date: "yesterday", "today" and "tomorrow". The child will say that something that happened six months ago happened yesterday.[7]
The child also misinterprets durations. Telling him to "come back in five minutes" has unpredictable results.[8]

items.question: my sisters husband died in the flood yesterday and she hasnt cried at all, is that normal? should i make her talk about it
matched: Not crying is normal and can be a sign of resilience; crying, laughter and silence are all normal
Do not press her to cry, to talk or to retell the loss; forced or excessive retelling can harm
Be there, listen when she wants to talk, give practical help
Keep her in the group and keep routine, food, sleep and useful activity going
Seek professional help when she cannot cope, is drinking or using drugs heavily, becomes very depressed, feels persistent guilt, feels life is not worth living or wishes she had died too
items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Grief
1. Expect grief to be messy and personal rather than a tidy set of stages. It is a long adaptation to living without someone, not a path to "recovery" by a date.
2. Crying is normal. Not crying is also normal and can be a sign of resilience. Laughter, celebrating the person, odd ways of coping, and even a sense of having seen or heard them are common, and most people find them comforting.
3. Do not press a grieving person to cry, to talk or to retell the loss; forced or excessive retelling can harm. Be there, listen when they want to talk, do not put down their grief or worry, give practical help, and put feelings into perspective gently.
4. Grieving people are often anxious. Keep them in the group, and keep routine, food, sleep and useful activity going, as for any stress reaction.
5. In a disaster, grief is complicated by not knowing. Use the family communication plan and safe-and-well registries to find out what can be found out.
6. Most people do not need professional help. Seek it, or help someone seek it, when they cannot cope, are drinking or using drugs heavily, become very depressed, can focus on little but the death, feel persistent guilt or that they should have prevented it, feel life is not worth living, or wish they had died too. Hospices, grief counsellors and peer groups such as networks for bereaved parents are places to start.
7. Writing about the loss and what it means has helped many people adjust; so can art and shared tasks. For children, see Keeping children calm.

The assistant adds:
Yes, your sister not crying at all is normal. Grief does not follow a predictable pattern or timeline; some people cry intensely, others don’t cry at all, and both are valid responses [1]. Not crying can be a sign of resilience or personal coping strategies—some individuals process loss through silence, humor, practical actions, or even laughter [1].

You should **not** make her talk about it. Pressing someone to share their grief or force them to cry can increase emotional distress and may harm the grieving process [1]. Instead:

1. Be present with her — sit quietly beside her if she wants company.
2. Offer practical help (e.g., meals, chores, running errands) so she feels supported without pressure to express emotions.
3. Let her know it’s okay not to cry or talk; your presence alone can be comforting [1].
4. If you notice signs of worsening distress—such as persistent sadness, inability to sleep, thoughts of self-harm, or feelings that life is no longer worth living—then consider gently suggesting professional help (like a grief counselor) when it becomes possible [1].

Grief adapts over time and varies from person to person. What matters most is her ability to feel safe and supported during this difficult time.

*Source: [1]*

sources.text:
1. Psychological first aid is as natural as physical first aid: helping someone in emotional distress, whether it comes from injury, illness or overwhelming stress. It needs no specialist training and goes hand in hand with treating wounds; fear and anxiety drain a person as surely as blood loss.
2. Look. Notice who needs help: the person who cannot function, is dazed, wandering, silent and withdrawn, or crying, screaming or raging. Someone confused and disoriented after a blow or a blast may have a head injury; treat it as medical until proven otherwise and keep them out of further danger.
3. Listen. Approach calmly and respectfully. Use their name. Accept their feelings without ridicule or blame; "snap out of it" and "it's all in your head" are hostility dressed as help. Let them talk if they want to, as often as they need to, and do not argue with their version of events. Never force anyone to retell what happened; debriefing people who have not asked for it does harm.
4. Link. Meet immediate needs: safety, warmth, water, food, a hot drink, attention to a small wound, accurate information about what is happening. Reconnect them with family and friends. Help them take one realistic next step. Connect them with medical, mental health or community services when needed, and offer to come back.
5. Once the first fear has passed, give them something useful to do: loading, clearing, carrying, minding children. Clear, simple, repeated instructions; respect their feelings but point them at the next obtainable task. Activity lets them forget themselves, releases tension and proves they can still do something.
6. Keep them with their group rather than alone; belonging restores security. Rest, sleep, food, water and clean clothes are treatment too.
7. Stay calm yourself. Your calm is the strongest medicine; if they see fear or anger in you, theirs grows. Expect them to recover and show it. Neither resentment of an injury you cannot see nor smothering pity helps.
8. If behaviour endangers them or others, do what is needed to keep everyone safe, keep someone they know with them, move them somewhere safer and get a medical assessment. Most reactions ease within hours or days.
Routine psychological first aid for everyone involved, including those who coped well, reduces later post-traumatic stress disorder.
sources.title: Psychological first aid

items.question: none of us have slept properly in 3 days since the earthquake, everyones making mistakes and snapping at each other. how do we fix it
matched: Make a household sleep plan: who is awake and watching, who sleeps, for how long
Make the sleeping place quiet, dark and cool, keep the same wake time, get daylight in the morning, and keep screens and bright light low before bed
No caffeine, nicotine or alcohol near bedtime; alcohol sends you off and then fragments the night
Nightmares soon after a frightening event are normal and fade; they are not a reason to avoid sleep; rebuild routine with fixed meal and bed times
missing: Lack of sleep cuts reaction time, judgment, memory and emotional control, and lapses cause accidents with vehicles, tools and fire; treat sleep as a safety item
