items.answer:
From the Field Guide, human-checked: Firecraft: building and lighting a fire that stays lit
Site
1. Find a dry spot out of the wind, close to your shelter but not under it or under low branches. Clear brush and scrape the ground to bare soil in a circle at least 1 metre across (3 metres where the ground is dry and grassy). Keep water or a shovel of dirt within reach.
2. If you can, build a low wall of logs or rocks on the windward side to reflect heat toward you and cut sparks. Never use wet or porous rocks; they can explode when heated.
3. On snow, lay two or three layers of green logs as a platform. For a hidden, fuel-saving cooking fire, dig a Dakota hole: a pit for the fire with a second hole angled in from the upwind side for air.
Material: collect three piles before you strike anything
Tinder catches from a spark: shredded inner bark, dry grass, birch bark, fine wood shavings, cotton lint, charred cloth. It must be absolutely dry; carry some in a sealed bag.
Kindling: pencil to finger thick dry sticks. Dead branches still on the tree are drier than wood lying on the ground.
Fuel: wrist thick and up. Seasoned, non-resinous hardwood burns longest. Gather more than you think you need and keep it dry; dry damp wood beside the fire.
Lay and light
1. Tepee: a cone of kindling around a fist of tinder; light the centre; it burns even damp wood. Lean-to: a green stick pushed into the ground at 30 degrees pointing into the wind, tinder under it, kindling leaned against it. Pyramid: layers of logs, each at right angles to and smaller than the one below, lit on top; it burns down unattended through the night.
2. Light from the upwind side. Shield the flame with your body. Feed small pieces as it catches; smothering a young fire with big wood is the usual failure.
3. Igniters: waterproof matches in a waterproof case with a striker; a lighter; a ferrocerium rod scraped with the back of a knife so the sparks land on tinder laid on a dry leaf; a magnifying lens or binocular lens in bright sun; a battery with two wires touched together over tinder. Flint on carbon steel (not stainless) works with practice. Friction methods (bow drill, fire plough) exhaust you; practise them at home, not in an emergency.
Keep it, then kill it
Bank the coals under ash to keep them alive overnight. Never leave a fire unattended.
To put it out: douse with plenty of water until the hissing stops, stir the ashes, add more water, and check that everything is cold to the touch. Where water is short, smother with sand or soil and then wet it. Never bury hot coals; they smoulder in roots for days.
Fire in a closed shelter makes carbon monoxide. Always leave a vent, and never sleep with a fire or stove burning in an unvented space.

The assistant adds:
1. Prepare your fire lay on dry ground out of the wind (at least 1 metre across), clear of brush and debris [1].  
2. Place a bundle of **dry tinder** under the V-shaped cut in the fire board — this is critical for catching sparks [5].  
3. Position one foot on the fire board to stabilize it, then loop the bowstring over the drill shaft [5].  
4. Insert the drill into the pre-cut depression on the fire board (this holds it steady) and place your hand on top of the drill socket to keep pressure applied [5].  
5. Begin sawing back and forth in a smooth motion — this twirls the drill, grinding hot black powder against the tinder to produce sparks [5].  
6. Apply **steady downward pressure** as you work; increase speed once a consistent motion is established [5].  
7. As sparks are generated, blow gently on the tinder to help it ignite (do not over-blow — this can extinguish small flames) [5].  

⚠️ **Warning**: The bow and drill method is exhausting and requires practice. If you're new to it or haven’t practiced at home beforehand, success in an emergency setting may be low [5].  
→ Try using a **ferrocerium rod** (scraped with the back of a knife) as backup — place sparks directly on dry tinder laid over a leaf for easier ignition.  

💡 *Note: Use non-aromatic seasoned hardwood for fuel and collect kindling/tinder along your trail in advance [5]. Add insect repellent to tinder if bugs are present.*  

If you continue having trouble, **stop trying** and switch to an igniter like waterproof matches or a lighter — the bow drill is not reliable under stress.  

*Source: [5] FM 21-76 Survival (US Army), page 70*

2. Light from the upwind side. Shield the flame with your body. Feed small pieces as it catches; smothering a young fire with big wood is the usual failure.

Site
1. Find a dry spot out of the wind, close to your shelter but not under it or under low branches. Clear brush and scrape the ground to bare soil in a circle at least 1 metre across (3 metres where the ground is dry and grassy). Keep water or a shovel of dirt within reach.
2. If you can, build a low wall of logs or rocks on the windward side to reflect heat toward you and cut sparks. Never use wet or porous rocks; they can explode when heated.
3. On snow, lay two or three layers of green logs as a platform. For a hidden, fuel-saving cooking fire, dig a Dakota hole: a pit for the fire with a second hole angled in from the upwind side for air.
Material: collect three piles before you strike anything
Tinder catches from a spark: shredded inner bark, dry grass, birch bark, fine wood shavings, cotton lint, charred cloth. It must be absolutely dry; carry some in a sealed bag.
Kindling: pencil to finger thick dry sticks. Dead branches still on the tree are drier than wood lying on the ground.
Fuel: wrist thick and up. Seasoned, non-resinous hardwood burns longest. Gather more than you think you need and keep it dry; dry damp wood beside the fire.

Ghosting is a visual artifact that occurs in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. This artifact can be a consequence of environmental factors or the human body (such as blood flow, implants, etc.). Ghosting is a multidimensional artifact that occurs in the MRI in the phase-encoded direction (short axis of the image) after applying the Fourier transform.
When the phase of the magnetic resonance signal is being encoded into the 2D or 3D Fourier image, a mild deviation from the actual phase and amplitude may occur. This incompatibility of parameters causes ghosting. The reasons this occurs are often physical factors, such as temperature or humidity of the environment, or movement caused by the patient or in the patient’s body.

To use the bow and drill, first prepare the fire lay. Then place a bundle of tinder under the V-shaped cut in the fire board. Place one foot on the fire board. Loop the bowstring over the drill and place the drill in the precut depression on the fire board. Place the socket, held in one hand, on the top of the drill to hold it in position. Press down on the drill and saw the bow back and forth to twirl the drill (Figure 7-8). Once you have established a smooth motion, apply more downward pressure and work the bow faster. This action will grind hot black powder into the tinder, causing a spark to catch. Blow on the tinder until it ignites.
Note: Primitive fire-building methods are exhaustive and require practice to ensure success.
HELPFUL HINTS
Use nonaromatic seasoned hardwood for fuel, if possible.
Collect kindling and tinder along the trail.
Add insect repellent to the tinder.

sources.text: The most recent version of the Broselow Tape incorporates updated length/weight zones based on the most current National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data set. Utilizing this data set to examine Broselow Tape predictions of actual body weight with the revised zones reveals that approximately 65% of the time the patient's measured length places them in the correct zone for actual weight. Of the remaining 35%, ~20% fall into the heavier Broselow-Luten zone above and 13% fall into the lighter zone below, with < 1% outliers falling greater than 1 zone from predicted. If the healthcare provider incorporates a visual estimate of body habitus into the prediction, the accuracy of the estimate of actual patient weight is improved, as confirmed in multiple studies.
